requirement: **GDScript Nullable Static Types**  GDScript shall support nullable static type annotations using the postfix `?` operator on any valid static type `T`, written as `T?`. The feature shall meet the following requirements:  1. **Syntax**: `T?` shall be accepted in all type annotation positions, including variable declarations, constants, function parameters, return types, signal parameters, lambda parameters, typed array element types (`Array[T?]`), typed dictionary key/value types (`Dictionary[K, V?]`), and nested combinations (e.g., `Array[Node?]?`). The `?` shall immediately follow the type expression.  2. **Semantics**: `T?` shall represent a value that is either `null` or a value of type `T`. `null` and values of type `T` shall be assignable to `T?`. `T?` shall not be implicitly assignable to `T`; conversion shall require an explicit null check, cast, or flow-sensitive narrowing.  3. **Non-Nullability**: A type annotation `T` without `?` shall be non-nullable. Assigning or returning `null` to/from a location of type `T`, or passing `null` as an argument to a parameter of type `T`, shall be a compile-time error. To preserve compatibility, existing code that violates this rule shall emit a deprecation warning before becoming an error in a subsequent release, or shall be supported through an explicit compatibility mode.  4. **Flow Analysis**: The static analyzer shall perform flow-sensitive nullability narrowing. After a check that proves non-null (e.g., `if value != null`, `if value is T`, `assert(value != null)`, or an early return on null), the value shall be treated as `T` within the guarded scope. Nullability shall be restored after assignments that may introduce `null`.  5. **Inference**: When no explicit annotation is provided, type inference shall infer `T?` for variables or return types whose initializer or returned expression may be `null`. The `null` literal shall infer the nullable form of the expected type in a typed context, or `Variant` when no context exists. Explicit annotations shall take precedence.  6. **Runtime**: Nullable annotations shall be erased at runtime and shall not change the runtime representation or behavior of values. No additional runtime checks shall be introduced solely for nullable types.  7. **Tooling**: The parser, analyzer, compiler, editor integration (autocompletion, type hints, documentation), and error messages shall recognize and display nullable types. Errors involving null-safety violations shall identify the offending expression, its nullable type, and the required null check or cast.  8. **Compatibility**: Existing scripts that do not use `?` shall continue to parse and run. The `T?` syntax shall not conflict with existing operators or syntax. The implementation shall provide a migration path for scripts that rely on implicit nullability of object types.

requirement: **Requirement: GDScript Method Overloading**  GDScript shall support user-defined method overloading in scripts and classes. A script or class may declare multiple methods with the same name when their signatures differ by parameter count or by the declared type of at least one parameter. Return type alone shall not distinguish overloads. Declarations with the same name that cannot be uniquely distinguished by parameter count and parameter type shall be rejected at parse/compile time with a clear diagnostic.  1. **Declaration and signatures**    - An overload signature consists of the method name plus the ordered parameter count and parameter types.    - Parameter names and default values shall not create a distinct overload signature.    - Overloads involving optional/default parameters shall be permitted only when all calls remain unambiguously resolvable; otherwise they shall be rejected at parse/compile time.    - The requirement applies to user-defined instance methods and static methods. It does not change operator overloading, built-in method binding, signal semantics, or constructor semantics unless separately specified.  2. **Overload resolution**    - A candidate overload is applicable when the supplied argument count matches its required and optional parameters and each supplied argument is assignable to the corresponding parameter type.    - For calls where argument types are statically known, the compiler shall select the unique most-specific applicable overload. A more-specific overload is one whose parameter types are subtypes of, or more specific than, another applicable overload’s parameter types. `Variant` and untyped parameters are applicable but shall lose to a more specific compatible overload.    - If no applicable overload exists, or if multiple applicable overloads are equally specific, the compiler shall raise a compile-time error identifying the method name, argument types, and candidate signatures.    - For calls where argument types are not statically known, overload resolution shall occur at runtime using the actual argument types and the same applicability and specificity rules. If no unique overload can be selected, a runtime error shall identify the method name, actual argument types, and candidate signatures.    - The declared return type of the selected overload shall determine the call’s static result type where known; otherwise the result type shall be `Variant`.  3. **Inheritance and dispatch**    - A derived class may add overloads to an inherited method name.    - A derived declaration with the same name and signature as a base method shall override that base method.    - A derived declaration with the same name but a different signature shall extend the overload set visible through the derived type.    - Calls made through a base-typed reference shall resolve against the base overload set, with normal virtual dispatch for overridden signatures. Calls through a derived-typed reference shall resolve against the combined derived and base overload set.  4. **Function references**    - Normal method-call syntax shall support overload resolution.    - Taking a `Callable` or method reference to an overloaded method name without enough context to determine a target signature shall produce a clear compile-time error, unless the implementation provides an explicit disambiguation mechanism that is documented.  5. **Compatibility and diagnostics**    - Existing GDScript code that does not declare overloaded methods shall continue to parse, compile, and run without behavioral change.    - Diagnostics for invalid declarations, unresolved calls, and ambiguous calls shall include the method name, supplied argument types, and relevant candidate signatures.  6. **Documentation and verification**    - The GDScript language reference shall document overload declaration rules, resolution rules, inheritance behavior, dynamic dispatch behavior, limitations, and error conditions.    - Automated tests shall cover: overloads differing by arity; overloads differing by parameter type; statically typed and untyped calls; `Variant` and untyped parameter specificity; optional/default parameter interactions; inheritance and virtual dispatch; ambiguous and invalid declarations; no-match and ambiguous-call diagnostics; `Callable` behavior; and regression coverage for non-overloaded methods.  **Acceptance criteria** - Given `func f(x: int)` and `func f(x: String)`, the call `f(1)` selects the `int` overload, `f("a")` selects the `String` overload, and an untyped call dispatches according to the actual argument type. - Given `func f(x: int)` and `func f(x: Variant)`, an `int` argument selects the `int` overload. - Given duplicate declarations with the same name, parameter count, and parameter types, compilation fails with a diagnostic. - Given an overload set where a call cannot be uniquely resolved, compilation or runtime execution fails with a diagnostic listing the candidate signatures. - A derived class can override a same-signature base method and add different-signature overloads, and calls through base- and derived-typed references resolve according to the inheritance and dispatch rules above.

requirement: # Requirement: Add TCP Keepalive Configuration to `TcpStream`  ## Summary Extend the `TcpStream` type in the `[libs]` crate with two public methods, `keepalive()` and `set_keepalive()`, that expose the underlying socket's TCP keepalive configuration. These methods allow callers to inspect and modify keepalive settings on an existing TCP connection, enabling detection of broken or idle peer connections at the transport layer.  ## Motivation TCP keepalive is a standard socket option used to detect dead peers and maintain long-lived connections through stateful network intermediaries. Currently, `TcpStream` users have no portable, safe way to read or write keepalive configuration without dropping to platform-specific raw socket APIs. Exposing this functionality aligns `TcpStream` with the socket-option coverage expected of a general-purpose networking primitive.  ## Functional Requirements  ### FR-1: `keepalive()` - **Signature:** `pub fn keepalive(&self) -> io::Result<Option<Keepalive>>` (signature may be adjusted to match crate conventions; accept `&self` receiver). - **Behavior:** Queries the socket for its current TCP keepalive configuration and returns it as a `Keepalive` value. - **Return semantics:**   - `Ok(Some(cfg))` when keepalive is enabled on the socket, where `cfg` reflects the current enabled state and any set duration/interval.   - `Ok(None)` when keepalive is disabled on the socket.   - `Err(e)` when the underlying `getsockopt` call fails (e.g., the socket has been closed or the platform does not support the query). - **Non-blocking:** The call must not block and must be safe to invoke on a non-blocking / async socket.  ### FR-2: `set_keepalive()` - **Signature:** `pub fn set_keepalive(&self, keepalive: Option<Keepalive>) -> io::Result<()>` (accept `&self` receiver). - **Behavior:** Applies the given keepalive configuration to the socket. - **Semantics:**   - `Some(cfg)` enables TCP keepalive with the properties described by `cfg`.   - `None` disables TCP keepalive. - **Return semantics:** `Ok(())` on success; `Err(e)` if the underlying `setsockopt` call fails. - **Non-blocking:** The call must not block.  ### FR-3: `Keepalive` type - Provide a `Keepalive` type (new or existing) that encapsulates:   - Whether keepalive is enabled.   - The keepalive time / idle duration (where supported by the platform).   - The keepalive interval / retransmission interval (where supported by the platform). - The type must be constructible, inspectable, and modifiable via public API (e.g., builder-style or accessor methods) so callers can express commonly needed configurations without touching platform-specific constants. - Where a platform does not support a particular property, setting it should either be a no-op on that platform or return an error; this behavior must be documented consistently.  ## Non-Functional Requirements  - **Portability:** Must compile and function on all platforms currently supported by the crate. Where a platform lacks a given socket option, the methods must degrade gracefully (documented behavior) rather than fail to compile. - **Safety:** Must be exposed as safe, idiomatic Rust; no `unsafe` in the public API surface. - **Consistency:** Method naming, receiver type, error type, and documentation style must match existing `TcpStream` socket-option methods (e.g., `set_nodelay`, `set_ttl`) in the crate. - **Documentation:** Both methods must carry doc comments describing parameter/return semantics, platform caveats, and interaction with async runtimes. - **Testing:** Include unit/integration tests covering:   - Enabling and disabling keepalive.   - Round-trip: `set_keepalive(Some(cfg))` followed by `keepalive()` returns an equivalent configuration on supported platforms.   - `keepalive()` on a socket with keepalive unset returns `Ok(None)` (or the platform's documented default).   - Error path on a closed socket.  ## Out of Scope - Automatic keepalive configuration on socket creation. - Changes to `TcpListener` or `TcpSocket` unless required to construct a `TcpStream` for testing. - Non-TCP transports (UDP, Unix domain sockets).  ## Acceptance Criteria 1. `TcpStream::keepalive` and `TcpStream::set_keepalive` are publicly exported and documented. 2. The methods compile without warnings on all supported targets. 3. On platforms with native keepalive support, a round-trip test demonstrates that a set configuration is readable via `keepalive()`. 4. On platforms without full support for a given property, behavior is documented and does not cause panics or undefined behavior. 5. Public API is reviewed against crate conventions and passes existing lint/CI checks.

requirement: # Requirement: Negative Trait Bounds  ## 1. Summary  Rust shall support expressing, in trait bounds, that a type parameter or concrete type does **not** implement a given trait. This capability ("negative trait bounds") shall allow library and application authors to write generic code that is only well-formed when a specific trait is absent, and to opt out of auto traits for specific types.  ## 2. Motivation  Today, trait bounds are purely positive: `T: Trait` states an obligation that must hold. There is no way to state the complementary obligation `T: !Trait`. As a result, authors cannot:  - Express mutually exclusive impl sets without relying on unstable `specialization` or fragile marker-trait workarounds. - Opt a specific type out of an auto trait that it would otherwise inherit structurally (e.g., a type that is `Send` by construction but must not be sent across threads). - Reject invalid type arguments at compile time with a clear message rather than allowing a downstream error to surface. - Encode "not this trait" constraints in generic APIs (e.g., "accept any `T` that is not `Copy`, so that move semantics are preserved").  ## 3. Functional Requirements  **FR-1 — Bound syntax.** The compiler shall accept a negative bound of the form `!Trait` wherever a trait bound is accepted today, including in: - generic parameter declarations: `fn f<T: !Clone>()`, `struct S<T: !Send> { ... }` - `where` clauses: `where T: !Iterator` - trait and impl definitions, including impl headers and associated type bounds.  **FR-2 — Well-formedness check.** A negative bound shall be enforced at type-check time. If a type argument is found to implement the negated trait, the compiler shall reject the item with an error that names the offending type, the trait, and the source location of the bound.  **FR-3 — Auto-trait opt-out.** For auto traits (`Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, and any user-defined `auto trait`), a negative bound or negative impl on a concrete type shall suppress the structurally derived implementation for that type and for types that contain it.  **FR-4 — Coherence interaction.** The compiler shall use negative bounds to determine impl overlap. Two impls shall not be considered overlapping when one is guarded by a negative bound that the other's type argument provably satisfies. Where overlap cannot be proven disjoint, the compiler shall emit a coherence error rather than silently accepting the impls.  **FR-5 — Inference behavior.** Negative bounds shall not be used to drive type inference. A negative bound shall be assumed to hold only when it is provable from a concrete type and the trait's known impls; unproven negative bounds shall not cause the compiler to select an impl. When the compiler cannot decide whether a negative bound holds, it shall report ambiguity rather than guessing.  **FR-6 — Conservatism / non-impl leakage.** Adding a new impl of a trait for an existing type shall be treated as a potentially breaking change with respect to any downstream negative bound on that type. The compiler shall detect and report such downstream breakage where it can be observed within the current crate graph.  **FR-7 — Diagnostics.** Violations shall produce actionable diagnostics, including: - a note identifying the positive impl that conflicts with the negative bound, - a suggestion to remove the bound or change the type argument, - a distinct error code for negative-bound violations.  **FR-8 — Stability gating.** The feature shall be usable only on the nightly channel behind a dedicated feature gate until it is stabilized. Use without the gate on stable shall produce the standard "unstable feature" error with the feature name.  ## 4. Non-Functional Requirements  **NFR-1 — Backwards compatibility.** All existing valid programs shall continue to compile and behave identically. No existing code shall acquire new errors solely from the presence of the feature.  **NFR-2 — Soundness.** Negative bounds shall not allow the construction of any program that would be rejected under the existing trait system's soundness guarantees (in particular, no unsound `Send`/`Sync` claims).  **NFR-3 — Compile-time cost.** Enabling negative bounds in a crate shall not cause more than a small constant-factor increase in trait-solving work for programs that do not use them.  **NFR-4 — Documentation.** The Rust Reference, the Rustonomicon (auto-trait chapter), and the standard error index shall be updated to describe the feature, its restrictions, and its failure modes.  ## 5. Acceptance Criteria  1. A test crate compiles where a generic function is constrained with `T: !Copy` and is instantiated only with non-`Copy` types. 2. Instantiating that function with a `Copy` type fails to compile with an error that names the type, the trait, and the bound's location. 3. A type marked with a negative `Send` impl is rejected when passed to a function requiring `Send`, and the error chain explains the negative impl. 4. Two impls distinguished solely by a negative bound on the same trait resolve to the correct impl for each type argument, with no coherence error. 5. A negative bound that cannot be resolved is reported as ambiguity, not silently accepted or rejected. 6. All pre-existing test suites in the compiler's test corpus pass unchanged with the feature gate enabled. 7. Feature-gate and diagnostics tests exist and are included in the standard test suite.  ## 6. Out of Scope  - Negative bounds on lifetimes. - Negative bounds on generic associated type projections where the projection is not yet resolvable. - Stabilization of the feature; this requirement covers the implementation and gating of the capability, not its final stabilization decision. - Changes to the surface syntax of positive bounds.  ## 7. Open Questions  - Whether negative bounds should be permitted in impl headers for coherence purposes in the initial implementation, or restricted to `where` clauses and function signatures first. - Whether an explicit `negative_impls`-style declaration and a `!Trait` bound should be unified into a single mechanism or remain two distinct, interoperating features.

requirement: # Requirement: Regular Expression Support in Test Filters  ## Summary The test filtering mechanism shall support regular expression (regex) patterns as filter criteria, in addition to the existing filtering capabilities, allowing users to select tests by matching test identifiers against user-supplied patterns.  ## Rationale Existing test filters require exact or partial literal matches, forcing users to enumerate individual test names or rely on limited wildcard syntax. This is impractical for large test suites where users need to select groups of tests sharing naming conventions. Regex support enables precise, flexible, and scalable test selection.  ## Functional Requirements  **FR-1 — Pattern Acceptance** The system shall accept a regular expression pattern as a test filter argument wherever test filters are currently supported (e.g., command-line options, configuration file entries, and programmatic APIs).  **FR-2 — Matching Semantics** A test shall be included in the run if its fully qualified identifier (as used by existing filters) matches the supplied regular expression. Matching shall be applied consistently to the same identifier scope used by existing literal filters.  **FR-3 — Match Mode** The system shall support both partial (search/unanchored) and full (anchored) matching, with the default behavior documented and consistent with existing filter semantics.  **FR-4 — Multiple Patterns** The system shall accept multiple regex filters in a single invocation. A test shall be included if it matches any supplied pattern (union semantics), consistent with existing multi-filter behavior.  **FR-5 — Combination with Existing Filters** Regex filters shall compose predictably with existing filter types (e.g., name, tag, path, exclude). The documented composition rules (intersection for inclusion filters, exclusion precedence for exclude filters) shall apply.  **FR-6 — Case Sensitivity** The system shall document and consistently apply case-sensitivity behavior, and shall support case-insensitive matching where the host language's regex engine provides it.  **FR-7 — Invalid Pattern Handling** On encountering an invalid or unsupported regex pattern, the system shall fail fast with a clear, actionable error message identifying the offending pattern and the reason for rejection, and shall not silently ignore the filter or run an unintended set of tests.  **FR-8 — No Match Behavior** If a valid regex pattern matches no tests, the system shall report this explicitly (consistent with existing empty-filter behavior) rather than silently passing or failing the run.  **FR-9 — Backward Compatibility** Existing literal and wildcard filter behavior shall remain unchanged. Regex support shall be opt-in via an explicit mechanism (e.g., a dedicated flag, prefix, or distinct option) so that existing filter inputs are not reinterpreted.  **FR-10 — Performance** Regex filtering shall not introduce significant overhead relative to existing filters; matching shall be performed against precomputed identifiers, and catastrophic backtracking shall be mitigated where feasible (e.g., via timeouts or engine limitations documented to users).  ## Non-Functional Requirements - **NFR-1:** Regex syntax and semantics shall follow the standard regex engine of the implementation language unless otherwise documented. - **NFR-2:** User-facing documentation shall describe syntax, anchoring, escaping, combination rules, and examples. - **NFR-3:** The feature shall be available across all supported interfaces (CLI, config, API) with consistent semantics.  ## Acceptance Criteria 1. A user can select a subset of tests using a regex pattern via the supported interfaces. 2. Anchored and unanchored matching behave as documented. 3. Multiple regex filters combine with union semantics; combination with other filter types follows documented rules. 4. An invalid pattern produces a clear error and a non-zero exit status (or equivalent failure signal). 5. A pattern matching zero tests is reported explicitly. 6. Existing literal/wildcard filters continue to behave identically. 7. Documentation includes syntax, examples, and combination rules.  ## Out of Scope - Replacement or deprecation of existing literal/wildcard filters. - Regex support in non-filter contexts (e.g., test output parsing or reporting).

requirement: **Requirement: Lint against unexpectedly late drops for temporaries in match scrutinee expressions**  The Rust Clippy lint suite SHALL include a warn-by-default lint named `significant_drop_in_scrutinee` that detects temporaries created in the scrutinee expression of a `match` expression whose destructor runs after the match arms execute because of Rust temporary lifetime rules.  The lint SHALL: - Trigger when a temporary in the match scrutinee has a non-trivial `Drop` implementation (e.g., lock guards, file handles, or other RAII types whose drop can block, perform I/O, or mutate shared state) and is not bound to a named local. - Emit a diagnostic at the scrutinee or temporary creation site explaining that the temporary is dropped at the end of the entire `match` expression rather than immediately after the scrutinee is evaluated, and that this can cause deadlocks, resource leaks, or borrow conflicts. - Provide a suggestion to bind the temporary to a local variable before the `match`, so the temporary’s lifetime ends before the match arms begin. - Avoid triggering for non-`Drop` types, for temporaries already bound to locals, or for scrutinees that do not introduce an extended temporary lifetime. - Respect standard Clippy lint controls, including `#[allow]`, `#[warn]`, `#[deny]`, and configuration through `clippy.toml` if applicable. - Include positive and negative UI tests covering lock guards, file handles, non-`Drop` values, bound locals, and match expressions in both statement and expression positions. - Produce no false positives on common Rust patterns where temporary lifetime extension is intentional or harmless.  Acceptance criteria: Running `cargo clippy` on code that creates a significant temporary in a match scrutinee produces the lint warning with a clear message and fix suggestion; running on code without such a temporary produces no warning.

requirement: **Requirement: Implement WebAssembly Garbage Collection (Wasm GC) in the Runtime**  The runtime shall support the WebAssembly GC proposal as standardized by the WebAssembly specification, enabling validation, instantiation, and execution of Wasm modules that use GC-managed reference types and instructions. Interoperate with existing runtime features, including reference types, typed function references, tables, globals, imports/exports, host functions, and data/element segments. Existing non-GC Wasm modules shall continue to execute unchanged. 6. Include comprehensive tests covering Wasm GC validation, instantiation, execution, allocation, collection, cyclic garbage, interoperability, and error cases. requirement: # Requirement: Support Images in Rustdoc Output ## 1. Summary Rustdoc shall render images referenced from documentation content (doc comments, doc attributes, and other rustdoc-processed markdown) in the generated documentation output, including images stored as local files relative to the documented source, without requiring the author to host them externally or to bypass rustdoc with `--html-in-header`. ## 2. Problem Statement Documentation authors currently cannot reliably embed images that live in the source tree. Relative image links in markdown do not resolve against the source file, and local image files are not copied to the rustdoc output directory, so images break in `cargo doc` output, in deployed docs, and on docs.rs. Authors work around this with external hosting (fragile, offline-hostile, privacy-sensitive) or by injecting raw HTML via `--html-in-header` / `--html-before-content` (not expressible in source, not portable across crates). ## 3. Scope In scope: - Markdown image syntax in `///` doc comments, `//!` crate/module docs, `#[doc = "..."]` attributes, and text pulled in via `#[doc = include_str!(...)]`. - Remote URLs, data URIs, and local file paths. - Copying referenced local image files into the rustdoc output tree. - HTML output and JSON output (`--output-format json`) content handling. Out of scope: - Image optimization, resizing, or format conversion. - Image generation or rendering of diagrams (e.g. Mermaid, PlantUML). - Images in doctest execution output. - Non-rustdoc documentation pipelines. ## 4. Functional Requirements **FR-1** — Rustdoc shall parse standard CommonMark image syntax (`![alt](url)`, `![alt](url "title")`) found in documented content and emit a corresponding `` element in HTML output, with `src` derived per FR-2 through FR-5, `alt` preserved verbatim, and `title` emitted as the `title` attribute when present. **FR-2** — Remote images (`http://`, `https://`, and protocol-relative `//`) shall be emitted unchanged as absolute `src` values. Rustdoc shall not fetch or validate them. **FR-3** — Data URIs (`data:image/...`) shall be emitted unchanged as `src` values. **FR-4** — Relative image paths shall be resolved against the directory of the file containing the markdown text, not against the process working directory, the crate root, or the path of the crate being documented. When the markdown text originates from `include_str!` or another include mechanism, resolution shall use the directory of the included file. **FR-5** — Every successfully resolved local image file shall be copied into the rustdoc output directory during documentation generation, and the emitted `src` shall reference the copied location. Copying shall: - preserve the reference as a valid relative URL from the rendered page, taking `--static-root-path` and resource layout into account; - preserve the file extension so browsers select the correct decoding path; - avoid path collisions between identically named files from different source directories by using a deterministic, collision-free destination layout; - apply URL percent-encoding for characters that are invalid in a URL path (e.g. spaces). **FR-6** — Supported local image formats shall be at minimum `.png`, `.jpg`/`.jpeg`, `.gif`, `.svg`, and `.webp`. Unrecognized extensions referenced from markdown shall still be copied and linked, or skipped with a warning, but shall not cause a hard error. **FR-7** — Reference-style image definitions (`![alt][id]` with `[id]: path`) and inline HTML `` in markdown shall resolve local paths using the same rules as FR-4/FR-5. **FR-8** — Resolution and copying shall work in all of: `rustdoc` invoked directly on a `.rs` file, `cargo doc`, documentation of workspace members, and documentation of a dependency (`cargo doc` for a dependency crate). Source file locations shall be obtained from `#[doc]` spans / source map information where available; when a source location is unknown, the path shall be treated as crate-root-relative and this fallback shall be documented. **FR-9** — When a relative image path cannot be resolved to an existing file, rustdoc shall emit a warning and render the markdown as an ordinary broken link or plain text. This shall not cause documentation generation to fail, and it shall not be a hard error under `-D warnings` unless the user opts in. **FR-10** — An unresolved-image diagnostic shall integrate with the existing rustdoc lint infrastructure so it can be allowed/denied/warned via CLI flags and `#![doc(...)]`-adjacent configuration, and shall report the source file and line of the reference. **FR-11** — Doctests extracted from documented content shall be unaffected by image syntax: images shall not be treated as code, and doc tests shall continue to be collected and run identically to the current behavior. **FR-12** — `--output-format json` output shall preserve the resolved (or unresolved) image `src` in the rendered markdown/HTML fragments it emits. Whether local image files are copied in JSON mode shall be documented behavior, and shall be consistent. **FR-13** — Cargo/Rustdoc shall expose a documented, stable mechanism (e.g. `--copy-images`/`#![doc(...)]` setting) to disable local image copying for consumers who manage assets themselves; when disabled, FR-5 copying is skipped and `src` values are emitted unresolved per FR-4. ## 5. Non-Functional Requirements **NFR-1 (Determinism)** — Given identical inputs, the set of copied files and their destinations shall be identical across runs and machines; no timestamps, absolute paths, or random identifiers shall leak into output paths or file contents. **NFR-2 (Performance)** — Copying shall be proportional to the number of distinct referenced local image files, not to the number of references. Re-running `cargo doc` without source changes shall not rewrite unchanged destination files (or shall do so only when content differs). **NFR-3 (No network)** — Documentation generation shall perform no network access for images. **NFR-4 (No new hard dependencies)** — The implementation shall reuse existing rustdoc/Pulldown-cmark infrastructure; any new dependency requires explicit design approval. **NFR-5 (Compatibility)** — Existing documentation that renders images via absolute URLs or data URIs shall be byte-identical in output, apart from any intentional resource layout changes. **NFR-6 (Accessibility)** — `alt` text from markdown shall always be preserved in the emitted ``; images with empty `alt` shall emit `alt=""`. **NFR-7 (Sanitization)** — Emitted `src`/`title`/`alt` values shall be HTML-escaped and shall not allow injection of arbitrary attributes or scripts from documentation content. ## 6. Acceptance Criteria 1. A doc comment `/// ![diagram](diagrams/flow.png)` on item `foo` in `src/lib.rs`, with `src/diagrams/flow.png` present, produces documentation whose rendered `` resolves to an existing copied file when served from the rustdoc output root. 2. The same source, but with the image at `src/a/b/flow.png` and a second `src/c/b/flow.png`, produces two distinct output files and two distinct `src` values; both images display correctly. 3. A doc comment containing `![logo](https://example.com/logo.png)` produces output identical to current behavior, with no copy performed and no network access. 4. A doc comment containing `![x](missing.png)` produces exactly one warning identifying the source file and line; `cargo doc` exits successfully. 5. A markdown file included via `#[doc = include_str!("docs/guide.md")]` that references `img/shot.png` resolves to `docs/img/shot.png`, and that file is copied. 6. A doc comment containing both a fenced Rust code block and an image yields the same set of doctests as before the change. 7. Running `rustdoc`/`cargo doc` twice with no source changes produces an identical output tree, and the second run does not modify copied image files. 8. `--output-format json` on a crate with image references completes successfully and the emitted content retains the image reference. 9. An image path containing a space (`![p](my image.png)`) renders an `` whose `src` is a valid percent-encoded URL that loads in a browser. 10. Documentation with existing absolute-URL and data-URI images produces output identical to the pre-change output. ## 7. Open Questions (to resolve before implementation) - Should resolution fall back to crate-root-relative when source span information is unavailable, or should such references warn? - Should `--static-root-path` users receive copied images under the static root or under the per-crate output directory? - Should file extensions outside the FR-6 list produce a warning or be copied silently?

requirement: **Requirement: Support Serving Go Modules from a Subdirectory of a Git Repository**  The `go` command shall support fetching and resolving modules whose module root is located in a subdirectory of a Git repository, rather than at the repository root.  Specifically:  1. When a module path includes a path suffix that corresponds to a subdirectory within a Git repository (e.g., a module path of `example.com/repo/sub/module` where the repository is at `example.com/repo` and the module resides in `sub/module`), the `go` command shall locate the repository, check out the appropriate revision, and use the contents of that subdirectory as the module root.  2. Version tags for such modules shall be recognized using the subdirectory-prefixed form (e.g., `sub/module/v1.2.3`) in addition to the standard form, consistent with the Go modules tagging conventions for nested modules.  3. Module zip archives and module source trees produced for such modules shall contain only the files within the subdirectory, with paths relative to the module root.  4. `go get`, `go mod download`, and `go list -m` shall correctly resolve versions, download, and verify such modules, including honoring the module's `go.mod` file located in the subdirectory.  5. The go command shall reject or report an error when the specified subdirectory does not exist at the requested revision or does not contain a valid `go.mod` file.  6. Existing behavior for modules located at the repository root shall remain unchanged.

requirement: **Requirement: Namespace Support in GDScript**  **Summary:** GDScript shall support namespaces so that classes, functions, constants, and enums declared in different modules or scripts can share the same identifier without collision, and so that related symbols can be grouped and referenced in a qualified form.  **Description:** Currently, all global class names (`class_name`) and autoloaded singletons share a single flat global scope. As projects and add-ons grow, name collisions occur, and third-party plugins cannot safely reuse common names. The language shall provide a namespace mechanism that:  1. Allows a script to declare the namespace it belongs to. 2. Allows symbols within a namespace to be referenced using qualified names (e.g., `Namespace.ClassName`). 3. Allows importing or aliasing a namespace to shorten qualified references within a script. 4. Preserves full backward compatibility: existing scripts without namespace declarations shall compile and behave identically.  **Functional Requirements:**  - FR-1: A script shall be able to declare a namespace, and all `class_name` declarations within it shall be registered under that namespace. - FR-2: Two classes with the same name in different namespaces shall coexist without error or ambiguity. - FR-3: Qualified references (`Namespace.Symbol`) shall resolve to the correct symbol at parse time where possible, and report a clear error when the symbol is not found. - FR-4: Unqualified references shall resolve first to the current namespace, then to imported namespaces, then to the global scope; ambiguous unqualified references shall produce a compile-time error. - FR-5: Namespaces shall support nesting (e.g., `A.B.C`). - FR-6: An import or alias mechanism shall allow a script to bring a namespace into local scope with an optional alias. - FR-7: Namespaces shall apply to functions, constants, enums, and inner classes, not only top-level classes. - FR-8: The editor shall provide autocompletion and go-to-definition for namespaced symbols. - FR-9: Namespace information shall be preserved in exported/serialized script resources and in `.tscn`/`.tres` references so that saved scenes resolve correctly after reload.  **Non-Functional Requirements:**  - NFR-1: Scripts without namespace declarations shall produce identical bytecode and runtime behavior to the current implementation. - NFR-2: Namespace resolution shall occur at parse/analysis time and shall not add measurable overhead to function calls at runtime. - NFR-3: Error messages for namespace-related issues shall identify the file, line, column, and the conflicting or missing symbol.  **Acceptance Criteria:**  - AC-1: Two plugins each defining `class_name Node` inside distinct namespaces load together without conflict. - AC-2: Referencing an undefined qualified symbol produces a compile error naming the namespace and symbol. - AC-3: An unqualified reference matching symbols in two imported namespaces produces an ambiguity error. - AC-4: The existing GDScript test suite passes unchanged. - AC-5: A scene referencing a namespaced script loads correctly after the project is closed and reopened. - AC-6: Editor autocompletion lists members of a namespace after typing `Namespace.`.  **Out of Scope:** Changes to C# or GDExtension name resolution; runtime dynamic namespace creation; automatic migration of existing projects to use namespaces.

requirement: ## Requirement: Lint against unexpectedly late drop of temporaries in a `match` scrutinee  ### Motivation  Temporaries that are created while evaluating the scrutinee of a `match` expression are kept alive until the *end of the whole `match` expression* — i.e. after the selected arm's body (and after any match guards) has run — rather than being dropped at the end of the scrutinee evaluation. This is frequently surprising, especially for types with meaningful `Drop` implementations such as `MutexGuard`, `Ref`/`RefMut`, `File`, `String`, `Vec`, or custom RAII types, because the user may reasonably expect the resource to be released before the arm body executes (e.g. to avoid holding a lock while doing work, or to release a file handle before the "done" message is printed).  The linter should make this behavior visible so that users can either accept it explicitly or restructure the code by hoisting the temporary into a `let` binding before the `match`.  ### Behavior  * The linter must inspect `match` expressions and determine whether the scrutinee expression creates one or more temporary values that:   * implement `Drop` (directly or transitively), and   * are not moved out of / bound by the match arms (i.e. are still owned by the temporary scope at the end of the `match`). * When such temporaries exist, a warning must be emitted, pointing at the offending temporary in the scrutinee. * The diagnostic message must state that the temporary is dropped at the end of the `match` expression (after the arm body/guard), and must suggest hoisting it into a `let` binding before the `match` if earlier release is intended. * The lint must be `allow`-by-default (e.g. in the `nursery`/`pedantic` group), and must be configurable through the standard lint attribute and configuration mechanisms (`#[allow(clippy::...)])`, `#[warn(...)]`, `#[deny(...)]`, and the `-A/-W/-D` command-line flags), including for the whole crate or a specific module. * The lint must not fire when:   * the scrutinee contains no temporaries with drop semantics (e.g. `match x { ... }` where `x: Copy` or is a plain binding);   * the temporary is explicitly bound by the arm patterns (e.g. `match mutex.lock().unwrap() { g if g > 0 => ... }` where the guard value is moved into the pattern) — in that case ownership is transferred and no late drop occurs;   * the temporary is explicitly dropped or `mem::forget`-ed by the user;   * the scrutinee is a `let`-bound variable or otherwise contains no temporary expression at all. * The lint should also recognize the equivalent `if let` and `while let` scrutinee temporaries, which exhibit the same late-drop behavior, or at minimum must not report false positives for them.  ### Examples  Lint (warning expected):  ```rust fn example(m: &Mutex<i32>) {     // The MutexGuard temporary is dropped only at the end of the `match`,     // i.e. after the arm body has run.     match m.lock().unwrap() {         0 => println!("zero"),         _ => println!("other"),     } } ```  No lint:  ```rust fn example(m: &Mutex<i32>) {     let guard = m.lock().unwrap(); // dropped at the end of this statement     match *guard {         0 => println!("zero"),         _ => println!("other"),     } } ```  No lint (value moved into the pattern, so no late drop):  ```rust fn example(m: &Mutex<i32>) {     match m.lock().unwrap() {         g if *g > 0 => println!("positive"),         _ => println!("other"),     } } ```  ### Implementation notes  * The check must be based on the typed AST/HIR of the scrutinee: collect the temporaries created in the scrutinee expression, keep only those whose type needs dropping, and exclude those whose ownership is moved by the arm patterns. * Temporaries that are dropped in a nested closure or in an inner scope must not be reported. * The diagnostic should be emitted once per offending scrutinee (not once per temporary) to avoid duplicate noise. * The lint must be documented in the linter's lint list with a clear title, explanation, and the before/after example above.
explanation: The requirement is precise and well‑structured, listing clear conditions, examples, and implementation notes that leave little room for multiple interpretations. Its verification criteria are concrete and measurable (e.g., detection of Drop temporaries, warning message content, lint configurability), making it straightforward to test. It defines a single linter feature—detecting late drops of scrutinee temporaries—with all additional details being refinements of that one capability, so it is singular.

requirement: # Requirement: Unified Data Reading Framework for PyTorch  ## 1. Title  Unified Data Reading Framework for PyTorch — multi-backend data source access (Hive, MySQL, S3, local filesystem)  ## 2. Motivation  PyTorch training pipelines currently require bespoke, hand-written data loaders per storage backend. Reading from Hive tables, relational databases (MySQL/PostgreSQL), or object stores (S3-compatible) typically means implementing custom `torch.utils.data.Dataset`/`IterableDataset` subclasses, duplicating logic for schema decoding, sharding across ranks, batching, shuffling, caching, credentials handling, and retries for every project. This results in duplicated code, inconsistent behavior across distributed workers, poor failure semantics, and tight coupling of training code to infrastructure details.  A single, declarative data reading framework is required that abstracts storage backends behind a common interface, exposing records to PyTorch as standard `Dataset`/`IterableDataset` objects so that training code remains backend-agnostic.  ## 3. Goals  1. Provide a single, stable Python API for reading training/inference data from heterogeneous backends (Hive, MySQL, S3, local filesystem) with no change to training code when switching backends. 2. Expose read results through standard PyTorch constructs (`torch.utils.data.Dataset`, `torch.utils.data.IterableDataset`, `DataLoader`) including native multi-worker and distributed (DDP/FSDP) support. 3. Support declarative configuration (Python API + YAML/JSON config file) so pipelines are reproducible and versionable. 4. Support distributed-aware sharding, deterministic ordering, and reproducible shuffling across ranks and workers. 5. Support schema inference and type conversion (SQL types ↔ Python types ↔ `torch` dtypes), plus composable record-level transformation pipelines. 6. Support pluggable backends so that new sources can be added without modifying framework core code.  ## 4. Non-Goals (Out of Scope)  - Not a data processing/compute engine (no Spark-like query planning, joins, or aggregation). - Not a replacement for `torch.utils.data.DataLoader`; the framework integrates with it rather than reimplementing it. - Not a feature store, dataset versioning system, or model/data governance platform. - Not a distributed training framework; it must be compatible with existing PyTorch distributed launchers. - Backend-specific advanced features (e.g., Hive ACID transactional semantics, MySQL stored procedures) are out of scope.  ## 5. Functional Requirements  ### 5.1 Core Abstraction  - **FR-1.** The framework shall define a `DataSource` abstract base class representing a readable data source, with at minimum:   - `schema` property returning a resolved schema (column name → type, nullable flag);   - `read(...)` / iteration method yielding batches of records;   - `get_reader(config)` returning a configured reader instance. - **FR-2.** The framework shall define a `Reader` interface responsible for producing batches for a given `DataSource`, split/shard specification, and runtime context (rank, world size, worker id). - **FR-3.** The framework shall define a `Backend` plugin interface with methods `open()`, `read_batch(...)`, `close()`, `infer_schema()`, enabling third-party extension by subclassing and registering via an entry point/decorator. - **FR-4.** The framework shall provide a public factory function (e.g., `read(source_spec)` / `build_dataset(spec)`) that returns a `torch.utils.data.Dataset` or `IterableDataset` object based on the source type and configuration. - **FR-5.** All public classes, functions, and configuration keys shall be importable from a single top-level package namespace with stable, documented names and semantic versioning guarantees.  ### 5.2 Backend Connectors  - **FR-6. Hive.** Support reading from Hive tables via ThriftServer/metastore or JDBC. Requirements:   - Column selection and predicate pushdown (partition predicates, WHERE clauses) where supported;   - Partition-aware scanning (e.g., `dt=YYYY-MM-DD`) with partition pruning;   - Schema inference from metastore with explicit type override support;   - Support for ORC/Parquet/sequence-file underlying formats via HiveServer2 or direct object-store access. - **FR-7. MySQL.** Support reading from MySQL tables/views. Requirements:   - Connection pooling with configurable pool size and lifetime;   - Cursor-based streaming reads (server-side unbuffered cursors) to avoid loading full result sets into memory;   - Support for `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT/OFFSET` clauses passed through from configuration;   - Consistent snapshot reads within a single reader instance where isolation level is configurable. - **FR-8. S3.** Support reading from S3 and S3-compatible object stores (MinIO, Ceph, R2). Requirements:   - Prefix/glob-based listing with optional recursive traversal;   - Support for CSV, JSON/JSONL, Parquet, and compressed variants (`.gz`, `.zst`, `.bz2`);   - Support for reading directly via `s3://` URIs in Hive/Hadoop-backed sources. - **FR-9. Local filesystem.** Support reading local files/directories using the same format handling as S3 for parity of behavior. - **FR-10.** Each backend shall be implemented as an independent plugin module; enabling/disabling a backend shall not require modification of framework core code or of other backends. - **FR-11.** Backends requiring optional third-party dependencies shall import them lazily and raise a clear, actionable error (naming the missing package and install command) rather than failing at package import time.  ### 5.3 Schema, Types, and Transformations  - **FR-12.** Schema inference shall be supported for all backends, with the ability to explicitly declare a schema in configuration to override inference. - **FR-13.** A type-mapping layer shall convert backend-native types to Python types and to `torch` dtypes, covering at minimum: integers (signed/unsigned, 8/16/32/64-bit), floats (16/32/64), booleans, strings/bytes, dates, timestamps, and nullable variants. - **FR-14.** Null values shall be represented consistently (e.g., `None`) and shall be convertible to framework-appropriate sentinels (e.g., `NaN`, `0`, or a configurable value) for numeric tensor columns. - **FR-15.** The framework shall provide a composable record-level transformation pipeline: `map`, `filter`, `select/rename`, `cast`, `fill_null`, `shuffle_buffer`, and `batch`. - **FR-16.** Transformations shall be composable in declaration order, and each stage shall be individually testable and inspectable. - **FR-17.** User-defined transformation callables shall receive a structured record/dict and return a dict, or a tensor/batch, and shall support both map-style (indexable) and iterable-style pipelines.  ### 5.4 PyTorch Integration  - **FR-18.** The framework shall return objects that are subclasses of, or fully interoperable with, `torch.utils.data.Dataset` and `torch.utils.data.IterableDataset`. - **FR-19.** Map-style datasets shall support `__len__` and `__getitem__` with configurable index-based or range-based access, including optional in-memory caching of the index metadata (e.g., row offsets) to avoid repeated scans. - **FR-20.** Iterable datasets shall implement `__iter__` yielding individual samples, and be compatible with `DataLoader(batch_size=..., collate_fn=...)`. - **FR-21.** The framework shall not require users to supply a `collate_fn` for common cases; a default collate supporting dict-of-lists and dict-of-tensors shall be provided, with the ability to override. - **FR-22.** Existing user-defined `collate_fn`, `sampler`, and `transform` hooks of `DataLoader` shall continue to work unchanged. - **FR-23.** The framework shall support `torch.utils.data.DataLoader` with `num_workers > 0`, including correct handling of worker seeding, per-worker reader instances, and cleanup of connections/cursors on worker termination. - **FR-24.** The framework shall support PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (and FSDP) by providing rank-aware sharding: each rank reads only its shard by default, with configurable sharding strategies (`by_row`, `by_file`, `by_partition`, `by_hash`, `round_robin`, `none`). - **FR-25.** Each dataset shall expose `set_epoch(epoch)` (and/or `__setstate__`/state-dict) so that shuffling and resharding can be made deterministic and distinct per epoch.  ### 5.5 Distributed Sharding and Determinism  - **FR-26.** Sharding shall be deterministic given `(source, split_spec, rank, world_size, epoch)`, producing a reproducible partition of records with no overlap and no omissions (verified by the test suite). - **FR-27.** A global seed shall control shuffling; the same seed with the same world size and epoch shall reproduce the same data order. - **FR-28.** Files/partitions shall be distributed across ranks in a balanced manner, and the framework shall expose per-rank record counts for verification. - **FR-29.** Support for reading a source once and broadcasting/broadcast-sharding to all ranks (e.g., small datasets) shall be provided via an explicit configuration option.  ### 5.6 Performance  - **FR-30.** Batch reads shall be supported natively by all backends (Hive fetch size, MySQL cursor fetch size, S3 range/list batching) to minimize per-record overhead. - **FR-31.** An optional bounded shuffle buffer and optional local disk cache/materialization layer shall be provided to improve throughput and reduce repeated remote reads. - **FR-32.** The framework shall expose read throughput metrics (records/sec, bytes/sec, latency percentiles) via an optional callback/logging interface. - **FR-33.** Where the backend supports it, predicate and column pushdown shall be used to reduce I/O; the framework shall not silently drop unsupported predicates but raise an explicit error when a requested predicate cannot be applied.  ### 5.7 Configuration  - **FR-34.** All sources and pipeline options shall be configurable via a declarative schema (Python dataclasses and/or YAML/JSON) covering: source type, connection parameters, credentials references, path/table patterns, format, read options, split/shard config, sampling, shuffling, caching, transformations, and batching. - **FR-35.** Secrets shall not be required to be stored inline in configuration files; the framework shall support environment-variable and external secret-provider references for credentials. - **FR-36.** Configuration validation shall occur at build time (before the first read) and shall raise a single aggregated error listing all invalid or missing fields. - **FR-37.** A resolved configuration object shall be serializable and printable (e.g., `to_dict()`/YAML dump) with secrets redacted, enabling logging of the effective configuration.  ### 5.8 Reliability and Error Handling  - **FR-38.** Transient failures (network errors, connection resets, throttling, 5xx responses) shall be retried with configurable exponential backoff and jitter, with a maximum retry count. - **FR-39.** Non-retryable errors (authentication failure, missing table/path, permission denied, malformed configuration) shall fail fast with clear messages that include the source identifier and the underlying cause. - **FR-40.** Readers shall implement proper resource cleanup (closing connections, cursors, file handles) on normal completion, exception, and worker shutdown; leaked resources shall not occur across repeated epochs. - **FR-41.** The framework shall emit structured warnings/errors for data-quality issues such as schema mismatch between inferred and actual data, truncated records, or parse failures, with a configurable policy to skip, quarantine, or abort.  ### 5.9 Observability and Logging  - **FR-42.** The framework shall integrate with the Python `logging` module and provide a consistent log format including source identifier, rank, worker id, and epoch. - **FR-43.** Optional progress reporting (records read, bytes read, ETA) shall be available via callback hooks and shall be safe to call from multiple workers (rank-0 aggregated by default).  ### 5.10 Extensibility  - **FR-44.** Third-party backends shall be registerable via a documented mechanism (decorator or `entry_points` group) without modifying framework source. - **FR-45.** A documented reference implementation of a custom backend shall be included, including a test harness, to lower the barrier for extension. - **FR-46.** The framework shall expose stable public interfaces such that internal refactoring does not break user code, enforced by semantic versioning and an API compatibility test.  ## 6. Non-Functional Requirements  - **NFR-1.** Python 3.9+ support; package shall be installable via `pip` and shall publish to PyPI. - **NFR-2.** Core framework shall depend only on `torch` and the standard library; each backend's third-party dependencies shall be optional extras (e.g., `pip install framework[hive]`, `[mysql]`, `[s3]`). - **NFR-3.** The framework shall not require a GPU and shall be usable in CPU-only environments. - **NFR-4.** Unit test coverage of ≥85% for core modules, and 100% coverage of sharding/splitting logic. - **NFR-5.** The framework shall maintain a documented minimum latency overhead per batch relative to a hand-written loader (≤10% for Parquet/CSV local reads). - **NFR-6.** All public APIs shall carry docstrings; user-facing documentation shall include quickstart, backend-specific configuration reference, distributed usage guide, and troubleshooting section. - **NFR-7.** CI shall run tests on Linux (and macOS/Windows where supported) across supported Python versions, including a distributed multi-process integration test using `torchrun`.  ## 7. Acceptance Criteria  1. A single configuration file can define a Hive table, a MySQL query, and an S3 prefix, and the same training script shall consume all three via `DataLoader` with only the configuration changing. 2. A user-written `collate_fn` and custom `torch.utils.data.Dataset` composition shall work without framework-specific code. 3. With `world_size=4` over a dataset of 1,000,000 rows, the union of shards read by all ranks contains each row exactly once, verified by an automated test. 4. Running the same configuration with the same seed twice produces byte-identical sample ordering. 5. A missing optional dependency (e.g., `pyarrow` for S3 Parquet) produces an actionable error message and does not prevent importing the framework or other backends. 6. Adding a new custom backend via the documented plugin interface requires no changes to framework core, and passes the supplied backend conformance test suite. 7. Credentials are never printed in logs or serialized configuration output.  ## 8. Deliverables  - Core package: source abstraction, reader abstraction, plugin registry, schema/type system, transformation pipeline, sharding/splitting, caching, config system, metrics/logging. - Backend plugins: `hive`, `mysql`, `s3` (with `local` filesystem support). - Public PyTorch integration API returning `Dataset`/`IterableDataset` implementations. - Configuration schema + YAML/JSON loader with validation and secret redaction. - Test suite: unit, integration (against local MySQL/Hive/MinIO test fixtures or mocks), distributed, and conformance tests for third-party backends. - Documentation: quickstart, backend guides, distributed guide, custom backend guide, troubleshooting, and an example project demonstrating end-to-end training over all supported backends.

requirement: **Requirement: MSVC COFF Object File Support in cmd/link**  The `cmd/link` tool shall support parsing, resolving, and linking Microsoft Visual C++ (MSVC) COFF (Common Object File Format) object files (`.obj`) to enable mixed-language linking scenarios, particularly for cgo on Windows platforms.  **Functional Requirements:** 1. **COFF Parsing**: The linker must parse COFF object files conforming to the Microsoft PE/COFF Specification, supporting architectures AMD64 (x86-64), 386 (x86), ARM, and ARM64. 2. **Section Handling**: Process standard COFF sections (`.text`, `.data`, `.rdata`, `.pdata`, `.xdata`, `.bss`, `.debug$*`, etc.), including COMDAT/section groups for proper deduplication of inline functions and template instantiations. 3. **Symbol Resolution**: Parse COFF symbol tables (including external, static, and section symbols with auxiliary entries) and integrate them with Go's symbol resolution system, ensuring correct handling of weak externals and common symbols. 4. **Relocations**: Support all relevant COFF relocation types per architecture (e.g., `IMAGE_REL_AMD64_ADDR64`, `IMAGE_REL_AMD64_REL32`, `IMAGE_REL_I386_DIR32`, etc.) and apply them during the linking phase. 5. **Import Handling**: Resolve references to the Import Address Table (IAT) and external DLL symbols for dynamic linking scenarios. 6. **Integration**: Seamlessly combine MSVC object files with native Go object files in the same link operation, maintaining existing dead code elimination and symbol visibility rules.  **Non-Functional Requirements:** - Must conform to Microsoft PE/COFF Specification version 8.0+. - Must maintain backward compatibility with existing Go object file formats and other supported input formats (e.g., Mach-O, ELF).

requirement: **Requirement: Support for Unsigned Fixed-Width Integer Types `uint16`, `uint32`, and `uint64`**  The system shall support the unsigned fixed-width integer types `uint16`, `uint32`, and `uint64` as first-class value types, with the following properties:  1. **Representation:** Each type shall occupy exactly 16, 32, and 64 bits, respectively, and represent values in the inclusive ranges 0 to 65,535, 0 to 4,294,967,295, and 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615. 2. **Literals and parsing:** The system shall accept integer literals and string inputs within each type's range and reject values outside that range with a descriptive error. 3. **Arithmetic:** Arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulo, and bitwise operations) on these types shall follow unsigned modular semantics or, where the host language or framework defines overflow as an error, shall raise a defined overflow error. The chosen behavior shall be documented and consistent across all three types. 4. **Conversions:** Explicit conversions between these types and other integer types (including `uint8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64`, and `size`/`usize`) shall be supported. Implicit narrowing conversions shall not be permitted. Widening conversions to larger unsigned or signed types shall be lossless. Conversions that may lose information shall require an explicit cast or an operation that reports out-of-range values. 5. **Serialization:** The system shall encode and decode these types in the supported formats (binary, JSON, and any other existing formats), using a defined byte order for binary formats and the decimal representation for text formats. Round-tripping a value shall produce an identical value. 6. **Interoperability:** Existing APIs that accept or return integer values shall accept these types where semantically appropriate without breaking existing signatures or behavior for current types. 7. **Error handling:** Out-of-range values, invalid conversions, and malformed serialized inputs shall produce specific, documented error conditions rather than silent truncation or undefined behavior. 8. **Testing:** The implementation shall include unit tests covering boundary values (0, 1, maximum value, and maximum value plus one where applicable), overflow and underflow behavior, conversion behavior, and serialization round-trips for all three types. 9. **Documentation:** The public documentation shall list the new types, their ranges, supported operations, conversion rules, and serialization formats. 10. **Compatibility:** Adding these types shall not change the behavior of existing code paths or existing public interfaces.

requirement: ## Requirement: PlatformView support on Windows  ### Context Flutter applications can embed native ("platform") widgets—such as web views, maps, video players, and native text inputs—into the Flutter widget tree via the `platform views` mechanism. This capability is currently implemented on Android and iOS but is missing on the Windows embedder. Windows users therefore cannot use packages that rely on `PlatformView` (e.g., `webview_flutter`, `google_maps_flutter`, `video_player`) and no equivalent exists for third-party Windows embedders.  ### Goal Provide first-class `PlatformView` support in the Windows embedder so that a Flutter app running on Windows can host native Win32/HWND child views within the Flutter rendering surface, with behavior and semantics consistent with the existing Android and iOS implementations.  ### Functional requirements 1. **Composition API parity**    - The Windows embedder and `flutter::PlatformView` infrastructure must expose a composition API equivalent to the Android/iOS `PlatformViewFactory`/`PlatformViewController` model.    - Provide a public API (C++ headers under `windows/flutter/`) allowing embedders to register a `PlatformViewFactory` keyed by a platform-view type identifier, and to create/destroy platform views on demand. 2. **View creation and lifecycle**    - When the framework requests a platform view of a given type, the registered factory is invoked with a creation parameters object carrying at least the view ID, the view type, and a JSON-encoded dictionary of arguments supplied by the Dart side.    - The created native view must be added as a child HWND to the Flutter view's host window, sized and positioned according to the framework-provided layout rect.    - The platform view must be resized/moved when the framework updates its layout, and hidden/shown when the framework toggles visibility.    - Platform views must be destroyed and their HWNDs released when the framework removes the corresponding widget, when the engine shuts down, and when the window is destroyed; no leaked handles or dangling callbacks. 3. **Input and focus handling**    - Mouse, keyboard, and IME input occurring over a platform view's bounds must be delivered to the native child view rather than to the Flutter framework.    - Pointer coordinates passed to the platform view must be translated into the child view's local coordinate space.    - Platform views must be able to take and relinquish keyboard focus, and focus transitions must be synchronized with the framework's focus model. 4. **Rendering integration**    - Platform views must be composited above the Flutter rendered surface (i.e., drawn after the Flutter layer) with correct z-ordering relative to other platform views and to Flutter-drawn content such as overlays.    - Platform views must not be painted over by Flutter content that is logically drawn on top of them, unless an explicit hybrid-composition mode is requested. 5. **Hybrid composition (optional/secondary)**    - Support a hybrid composition mode in addition to virtual display composition, so that platform views may participate in Flutter's scene graph (e.g., for effects and clipping) while still hosting a native child window. 6. **Tooling and package support**    - The `flutter/packages` web-view and text-input implementations, and any other in-tree packages that use platform views, must be able to render their native equivalents on Windows.    - `flutter create` templates and the Windows runner must build and run without modification on Windows.  ### Non-functional requirements - No measurable regression in rendering performance or frame rate for apps that do not use platform views. - Correct behavior across DPI scaling levels, window resizing, minimization/restore, and monitor changes. - The implementation must pass the shared `flutter/platform_views` integration tests, and equivalent Windows-specific tests must be added covering creation, resizing, input routing, focus, and disposal.  ### Acceptance criteria 1. A sample Flutter app on Windows embeds a native platform view (e.g., a Win32 child window displaying a native control) at a specified position and size, and the native content appears correctly composited over the Flutter canvas. 2. Resizing the Flutter window resizes and repositions the platform view proportionally to its layout rect. 3. Mouse clicks and keyboard input over the platform view are received by the native view and not by the Flutter framework. 4. Removing the platform-view widget from the Dart tree destroys the native child window and releases all associated resources. 5. The same app runs on Android, iOS, and Windows without platform-conditional Dart code (beyond platform-specific factory registration). 6. `flutter test` and the platform-view integration test suite pass on Windows with no skipped or failing cases.

requirement: # Requirement: Run `compute()` on a Separate Thread (Web Worker) in Flutter Web  ## 1. Background / Problem  `compute()` from `package:flutter/foundation.dart` is the canonical way for Flutter applications to offload CPU-bound work (e.g. JSON parsing, image processing, encryption) off the UI thread by executing it in a background isolate. On mobile and desktop targets this is implemented with `dart:isolate` and executes on a genuinely separate OS thread.  On the web, there is no OS thread model and `dart:isolate`'s `Isolate.spawn` is unsupported. The current web implementation of `compute()` executes the supplied callback **inline on the main UI thread** (or otherwise degrades to synchronous execution), so:  - Long-running callbacks **block rendering and input handling**, causing visible jank/frozen frames. - Developers get no performance benefit from `compute()` on web, and cross-platform code that relies on `compute()` for responsiveness silently regresses. - Platform behavior is inconsistent: the same source code behaves differently on web vs. native, which is a correctness and API-parity defect.  ## 2. Goal  Make `compute()` (and the isolate-style background execution API surface exposed by `package:flutter`) execute the caller's callback on a **separate thread** in Flutter Web by leveraging **Web Workers**, preserving the same semantics, error reporting, and API contract as the native (IO) implementation.  ## 3. Scope  **In scope**  - `package:flutter/foundation.dart` → `compute()` on web targets. - The underlying isolate/worker abstraction used by the framework (worker creation, message passing, termination, error propagation). - Support for all Flutter web compilation modes (debug, profile, release, `dart2js` and `dart2wasm`/WasmGC builds). - Framework-side documentation and changelog updates, plus public-API documentation clarifying web behavior.  **Out of scope**  - Adding general-purpose `dart:isolate` support to the Dart web SDK (this requirement consumes worker-based background execution; a full `dart:isolate` web implementation is a separate SDK-level effort). - Unstructured concurrency (`Isolate.run` with arbitrary closures/async gaps) unless it can be supported without breaking existing web semantics. - GPU/OffscreenCanvas-based compute offload. - Changes to native (IO) behavior.  ## 4. Functional Requirements  ### FR-1 — True off-thread execution - `compute<T, R>(ComputeCallback<T, R> callback, T message)` on web MUST execute `callback` inside a Web Worker (a dedicated background thread), never on the main UI thread. - The main thread MUST remain responsive (able to process frames and input events) while the callback is running.  ### FR-2 — API and semantic parity with native - The web implementation MUST match the native contract for:   - Calling `callback` exactly once per `compute()` invocation.   - Completing the returned `Future<R>` exactly once with the callback's return value.   - Propagating errors thrown by the callback to the caller. - `compute()` MUST remain usable without any web-specific API changes at call sites; existing code must not require modification to gain the benefit.  ### FR-3 — Message and result serialization - The `message` argument and the callback's return value MUST be transferable between the main thread and the worker. - Supported types MUST include, at minimum: `null`, `bool`, `int`, `double`, `String`, `List`, `Map`, `Set`, `Uint8List`, and other `TypedData`/`TransferableTypedData` types. - Types that cannot be transferred (e.g. arbitrary class instances, closures, `ReceivePort`s) MUST produce a clear, actionable error consistent with the native implementation's "not sendable" error behavior — the operation MUST NOT hang and MUST NOT silently produce a wrong result.  ### FR-4 — Error propagation - An uncaught exception thrown inside the worker MUST be surfaced to the `compute()` caller as an error with:   - The original error message and type where available.   - The original stack trace (or the worker-side stack trace) preserved in the resulting error's `stackTrace`. - Errors MUST be distinguishable from transport/protocol failures.  ### FR-5 — Worker lifecycle and resource management - Worker startup MUST be amortized: the framework SHOULD reuse a worker (or a small pool of workers) across `compute()` calls rather than paying full worker instantiation cost on every call, while still guaranteeing that a single `compute()` invocation runs in exactly one worker context. - Workers MUST be terminated and their resources released when no longer needed, and MUST NOT accumulate indefinitely over the application's lifetime. - Terminating or tearing down a worker MUST NOT leave the caller's `Future` unresolved; pending futures MUST be completed with an error.  ### FR-6 — Graceful degradation / unsupported environments - If the environment cannot create a Web Worker (e.g. blocked by a Content Security Policy that disallows `worker-src`/`blob:` workers, or a non-browser host), `compute()` MUST either:   - fall back to synchronous inline execution with a documented, debug-visible warning, or   - fail with a descriptive `UnsupportedError` naming the cause,   and the chosen behavior MUST be consistent and documented. - The fallback path MUST be surfaced in debug builds (e.g. via `debugPrint`/assertion) so developers are not misled into believing off-thread execution occurred.  ### FR-7 — Build-mode and tooling compatibility - The implementation MUST work in debug, profile, and release web builds, and with both `dart2js` and `dart2wasm` compilation targets. - The worker bootstrap code MUST be bundled/emitted correctly by the web toolchain (including code-splitting/route-based lazy builds) and MUST NOT require the application author to add extra files, `web/` directory entries, or asset declarations to their project. - Worker source maps SHOULD be preserved in debug/profile builds.  ### FR-8 — Observability and diagnostics - Debug builds SHOULD provide a way to observe worker creation, reuse, execution time, and termination (e.g. verbose logging behind a flag), to aid performance analysis.  ## 5. Non-Functional Requirements  | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | NFR-1 | Main-thread blocking time attributable to `compute()` invocation overhead MUST be bounded and small relative to the work offloaded; overhead MUST be measured and published. | | NFR-2 | No measurable regression in startup time, rendering performance, or memory footprint for applications that do not use `compute()`. | | NFR-3 | Thread safety: no shared mutable state between main thread and worker; all communication via message passing with the documented type allow-list. | | NFR-4 | Security: workers MUST be same-origin and MUST NOT use `eval`-based workarounds that would violate a strict CSP without an explicit, documented opt-in. | | NFR-5 | Compatibility with the officially supported browser matrix (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, and mobile equivalents), including browsers where worker startup cost is high. | | NFR-6 | The feature MUST be opt-in-free for callers (no new required API) but MAY be gated internally behind an experimental flag until stabilized. | | NFR-7 | The implementation MUST be testable in the framework's automated test infrastructure (unit, integration, and web-specific browser tests). |  ## 6. Acceptance Criteria  **AC-1 — Off-thread execution** - **Given** a Flutter web app that calls `compute()` with a callback that busy-loops for ~2 seconds, - **When** the callback is running, - **Then** the UI continues to render and respond to input (frame timings show no multi-second stall), and the callback's thread/worker identity differs from the main thread's.  **AC-2 — Result correctness** - **Given** `compute()` with a callback returning a complex serializable structure (nested maps/lists, `Uint8List`), - **When** it completes, - **Then** the returned value is deep-equal to the expected structure and byte-identical for binary payloads.  **AC-3 — Error propagation** - **Given** a callback that throws a custom exception with a message, - **When** `compute()` is awaited, - **Then** the future completes with an error containing the original message and a non-empty stack trace referencing the callback.  **AC-4 — Non-sendable argument** - **Given** `compute()` invoked with an argument that cannot be transferred, - **When** the call is made, - **Then** it fails fast with a descriptive error and does not hang.  **AC-5 — Repeated use / no leaks** - **Given** an app that calls `compute()` 1,000 times sequentially, - **When** the calls complete, - **Then** all futures complete correctly, and the number of live workers remains bounded (reused or pooled), with no unbounded growth in worker count or memory.  **AC-6 — Unsupported environment** - **Given** a page whose CSP forbids worker creation, - **When** `compute()` is invoked, - **Then** the documented fallback or `UnsupportedError` occurs, and a diagnostic is emitted in debug mode.  **AC-7 — Cross-platform parity** - **Given** an identical application source using `compute()`, - **When** built for web and for a native target, - **Then** the observable API behavior (result values, error semantics, call counts) matches.  **AC-8 — Regression safety** - **Given** an application that never calls `compute()`, - **When** built for web, - **Then** bundle size, startup time, and rendering performance are unchanged within the tolerance defined by the web performance benchmarks.  ## 7. Documentation & Communication Requirements  - Update the API documentation for `compute()` to state explicitly that on web the computation runs in a Web Worker (separate thread) and list the transferable/serializable types. - Add a release note / changelog entry describing the new web behavior, including any behavior differences from native. - Publish guidance for developers whose deployments restrict workers (CSP) describing the fallback behavior and required CSP directives. - Provide a migration note for anyone relying on the previous inline-execution behavior on web (e.g. code that depended on synchronous side effects).  ## 8. Open Questions  1. Should `compute()` on web default to a **single shared worker** (serialized execution) or a **worker pool** (parallel execution) when multiple `compute()` calls are in flight concurrently? 2. What is the exact fallback contract when workers are unavailable: silent inline execution with a warning, or a hard `UnsupportedError`? 3. Is `Isolate.run`/`Isolate.spawn`-style API exposure in scope for web in a follow-up, or is `compute()` the sole supported surface? 4. What is the acceptable per-call overhead target for worker message round-trips given worker startup cost on Safari? 5. Should worker usage be made observable via `Timeline`/performance overlay events in debug builds?
