requirement: # Requirement: WebGPU Support  ## 1. Overview  Add first-class support for the WebGPU API as a rendering backend, alongside the existing rendering path(s), enabling the project to run on WebGPU-capable browsers/agents while preserving current functionality and performance on platforms where WebGPU is unavailable.  ## 2. Motivation  WebGPU is the successor to WebGL for GPU-accelerated content in the browser. Supporting it provides modern GPU features (compute shaders, storage buffers, timestamp queries, bindless resources), lower CPU overhead, and access to features unavailable in WebGL. It also future-proofs the project against deprecation of WebGL in target environments.  ## 3. Scope  ### 3.1 In Scope  - A pluggable renderer/backend abstraction that allows a WebGPU implementation to be selected at runtime. - Automatic or explicit selection of the WebGPU backend based on feature detection and user/host configuration. - A complete WebGL-equivalent rendering path implemented on top of WebGPU (all currently supported rendering features must work under WebGPU with no visual or behavioral regressions). - Graceful, deterministic fallback to the existing backend when WebGPU is unavailable, unsupported, or fails to initialize. - Configuration, build, packaging, documentation, telemetry/diagnostics, and automated test coverage.  ### 3.2 Non-Goals  - Exposing new user-visible rendering features exclusive to WebGPU in this change (beyond parity with existing features), except where required for parity. - Implementing compute-shader-based rendering pipelines or advanced GPU features not required for parity. - Removing or deprecating the existing backend. - Supporting WebGPU in environments that expose only WebGL (no behavior change there). - Native/headless GPU drivers beyond those already used by the existing backend.  ## 4. Terminology  - **Backend**: an implementation of the rendering abstraction (existing backend(s) and the new `webgpu` backend). - **Adapter**: a physical or logical GPU exposed by the WebGPU implementation (`GPUAdapter`). - **Device**: a `GPUDevice` obtained from an adapter, used for resource creation and command submission. - **Surface/Context**: the presentation target onto which the WebGPU backend renders (e.g., `GPUCanvasContext`).  ## 5. Functional Requirements  ### FR-1: Backend Abstraction  The rendering code must be expressed against a backend-neutral interface. All direct WebGL/WebGPU calls must be confined to backend-specific implementations. The abstraction must support, at minimum: resource/texture creation and upload, buffer creation and update, shader/program compilation, pipeline/state creation, framebuffer/render-target binding, draw submission, and presentation.  ### FR-2: Initialization & Device Acquisition  The WebGPU backend must, on start-up:  1. Check for the presence of `navigator.gpu` and request an adapter (`requestAdapter`) with an explicit power-preference policy derived from project configuration (default: `high-performance` with fallback to `low-power`, then to any adapter). 2. Request a `GPUDevice` with only the features and limits required by the backend, using `requiredFeatures`/`requiredLimits` derived from actual usage (no blanket requests of optional features). 3. Handle `requestAdapter()` returning `null` and `requestDevice()` rejecting (including `device.lost`) as initialization failures. 4. Report initialization outcome through the project's existing initialization/status reporting mechanism, including a machine-readable reason for failure.  ### FR-3: Context & Presentation Configuration  The backend must configure the presentation context (`configure`) with an explicit `format` selected from `navigator.gpu.getPreferredCanvasFormat()` (or an explicit override), an appropriate `alphaMode`, and a usage set including at least `RENDER_ATTACHMENT`. The backend must handle canvas resize, device-pixel-ratio changes, and context reconfiguration without leaking resources or presenting stale frames.  ### FR-4: Resource Parity & Lifecycle  - Textures, buffers, and samplers created through the abstraction must behave equivalently to the existing backend, including color-space handling, premultiplied alpha, filtering, wrapping, and mipmap generation. - All GPU resources must be released deterministically via the abstraction's disposal path; no `GPUBuffer`/`GPUTexture` may be leaked across frame boundaries or on teardown. The backend must track owned resources so that backend teardown frees them all. - Missing support for a required WebGPU feature/limit must be detected at initialization and surfaced as an error rather than failing mid-frame.  ### FR-5: Shader & Pipeline Compilation  - Shaders must be authored in a form usable by both backends (e.g., WGSL with a translation step, or a shared intermediate representation), with no hand-maintained duplicate shader sets where avoidable. - Program/pipeline creation must be asynchronous-friendly: the backend must not block the main thread synchronously on `createRenderPipeline`/`createShaderModule` for more than the project's existing budget, and must expose compilation errors (including `getCompilationInfo()` messages) through the project's existing error-reporting facility. - Shader compilation errors must be surfaced with file/line information sufficient to locate the offending source.  ### FR-6: Frame Rendering  - The backend must submit work using a single command encoder per frame (or per documented batching unit), with render passes matching the existing backend's pass structure. - It must correctly handle render-target switches, clears, depth/stencil testing, blending, scissor/viewport state, and draw-call ordering. - It must implement a resource-cleanup pass (e.g., `GPUTexture.destroy()`, buffer `destroy()`) invoked according to the existing frame lifecycle. - Uncaptured errors and validation errors (`device.onuncapturederror`, error scopes) must be captured, logged with context, and surfaced to the developer-facing error overlay/console in the same manner as existing backend errors.  ### FR-7: Backend Selection & Fallback  - Selection order must be deterministic and configurable: explicit user/host setting (e.g., `?renderer=webgpu`, config option, or feature flag) → automatic detection → existing backend. - Automatic detection must select WebGPU only when `navigator.gpu` exists **and** an adapter and device are successfully obtained. - If the WebGPU backend fails at any point during initialization or during the first N frames (N configurable, default 1), the application must fall back to the existing backend transparently, re-initializing presentation state, without a page reload and without user-visible corruption. - The selected backend must be discoverable at runtime (e.g., reported in the existing debug/status overlay or exposed via a public API/property) so that users and tests can assert which backend is active. - Backend selection must be reported to the project's existing telemetry/analytics mechanism, if one exists, in compliance with its privacy policy (no new identifiers, no fingerprinting).  ### FR-8: Configuration & Build  - WebGPU support must be behind a build/runtime flag that can be disabled without code changes to the core (e.g., bundler define/environment variable plus a runtime option). - The build must not fail in environments lacking WebGPU typings/declarations; TypeScript types for WebGPU must be included and correct, with no `any`-typed escape hatches in the backend's public surface. - The bundle must not include duplicate copies of the WebGPU shader translation layer; tree-shaking must remain effective.  ### FR-9: Compatibility & Degradation Matrix  The following must be verified and documented:  | Environment | Expected behavior | |---|---| | Browser with WebGPU enabled | WebGPU backend active | | Browser without WebGPU | Existing backend active, no console errors | | Browser with WebGPU present but adapter request fails | Existing backend active, reason reported | | WebGPU device lost mid-session | Recovery attempt, then fallback to existing backend, error surfaced | | Safari / Firefox (WebGPU support status varies) | Per current support level; no crash; documented behavior |  ### FR-10: Documentation  - Document: how to enable/disable the WebGPU backend, how to force a specific backend for debugging, the support matrix, known limitations, and troubleshooting steps for common errors (e.g., "device lost", "adapter null"). - Update the project's README and/or docs site with a WebGPU section. - Any behavioral difference from the existing backend that users can observe (e.g., color/alpha handling, antialiasing, texture filtering) must be documented.  ### FR-11: Testing  - Unit tests covering backend selection logic, capability/feature detection, fallback triggers, and resource disposal bookkeeping. - Integration tests that render a deterministic reference scene under both backends and compare output against golden images with a documented, per-platform tolerance. - An automated test that runs in a WebGPU-capable environment and asserts the WebGPU backend is selected and a frame is presented successfully (skipped, not failed, when WebGPU is unavailable). - Tests must not be flaky: any timing-sensitive behavior must use deterministic synchronization (e.g., `queue.onSubmittedWorkDone()`, `mapAsync`) rather than arbitrary timeouts.  ## 6. Acceptance Criteria  1. WebGPU can be enabled via configuration and, where supported by the environment, is selected automatically. 2. All features currently supported by the existing backend render correctly under WebGPU with no visual regressions beyond documented, justified differences. 3. When WebGPU is unavailable or fails to initialize, the application runs on the existing backend with no uncaught exceptions and no user-visible failure. 4. No GPU resource leaks: repeated create/destroy cycles (≥1000 iterations) do not increase retained resource counts beyond a documented threshold, verifiable via `device` resource accounting or the browser's memory tooling. 6. Frame time and frame rate under WebGPU are not materially worse than the existing backend on the reference hardware (within an agreed margin, e.g., ≤5% median regression), or the difference is documented with justification. 7. The active backend is introspectable at runtime and covered by automated tests. 8. The WebGPU backend code passes the project's linting, type checking (strict mode, no `any` in backend public API), and code review standards. 9. Documentation listed in FR-10 is merged.  ## 7. Constraints & Assumptions  - The project targets browsers/agents with a standards-compliant WebGPU implementation; experimental or vendor-prefixed implementations are out of scope. - The existing rendering abstraction can be extended to support the parity requirements without a breaking change to the public API. - Shader sources can be shared or mechanically translated between backends; if a full translation is not feasible, maintaining parallel shader sets is acceptable provided they are generated, not hand-duplicated. - Telemetry changes are limited to reporting backend selection and must not introduce new data collection.  ## 8. requirement: # Requirement: INT4 (4-bit Integer) Format Support  ## 1. Summary  Add native support for the **INT4** data format — a 4-bit quantized integer tensor type — to the project's quantization, storage, and inference stack. INT4 tensors must be creatable, quantized from floating-point tensors, dequantized back to floating point, persisted to disk/serialized formats, and consumed by kernels and framework bindings alongside the already-supported lower-precision formats (e.g., INT8).  ## 2. Motivation  - 4-bit weights halve the memory footprint of INT8 and reduce it 4× relative to FP16, enabling larger models to fit on consumer GPUs/CPUs and reducing model-load I/O. - INT4 is the de-facto standard for weight-only compression in the ecosystem (GPTQ, AWQ, GGML/GGUF `Q4_*` families); native support removes the need for external conversion steps and format-shim kernels. - A first-class `INT4` type lets users select INT4 explicitly and gives the runtime a single, well-documented representation to target with optimized kernels.  ## 3. Scope  ### 3.1 In Scope  - A registered `INT4` tensor/data type with well-defined semantics (packing, block layout, scale/zero-point handling). - Quantization of floating-point tensors (FP32/FP16/BF16) to `INT4`, and dequantization of `INT4` back to floating point. - Support for both **symmetric** (scale-only) and **asymmetric** (scale + zero-point) quantization modes. - Configurable block size and scale data type. - Serialization/deserialization of `INT4` tensors in the project's model/weight file format, including all metadata required for faithful reconstruction. - Kernel-level support for operations that read `INT4` inputs (notably dequantize-to-FP16/FP32 and quantized linear/matmul paths), with correct fallback to dequantize-then-compute where no fused kernel exists. - Public API exposure (Python and C/C++/native library, as applicable) plus command-line tooling for conversion and inspection. - Unit, integration, accuracy, and round-trip tests.  ### 3.2 Out of Scope (this iteration)  - INT4 activations for all operators (activation quantization remains as currently supported). - Mixed INT4/INT8 or per-tensor "grouped" schemes beyond a single configurable block size. - Training / fine-tuning with INT4 gradients. - Hardware-specific INT4 tensor-core paths beyond generic implementations (may be added later as optimizations).  ## 4. Definitions  | Term | Definition | |---|---| | `INT4` | Tensor element type holding 4-bit two's-complement signed integers, range `[-8, 7]`. | | Block | Contiguous group of elements sharing one scale (and zero-point). Default block size **32**. | | Scale | Multiplier of type `F16` (default) or `F32`, applied per block. | | Zero-point | Integer offset of type `INT4`-domain (default `0`; used only in asymmetric mode). | | `q` | Stored quantized integer value for an element. | | `x` | Original floating-point element. | | Packed byte | Two 4-bit values stored in one byte: low nibble = even index, high nibble = odd index, little-endian byte order within the file. |  ## 5. Functional Requirements  ### FR-1: Type Registration  - **FR-1.1** Register `INT4` (aliases accepted: `int4`, `i4`, `q4`) in the global type/dtype registry alongside existing integer and quantized types. - **FR-1.2** The registered type must expose: bit width (4), signedness (signed), element byte size for accounting purposes (0.5, reported as `itemsize = 0.5`), block size, scale type, and a human-readable name (e.g., `"INT4"`). - **FR-1.3** The type must be selectable wherever a dtype is currently selectable (constructor arguments, `astype`/`to()` calls, config files, CLI flags, serialization header, framework bindings). - **FR-1.4** Type metadata (block size, scale dtype, symmetric flag, zero-point presence) must be carried with the tensor/container, not inferred globally.  ### FR-2: Quantization  - **FR-2.1** Provide `quantize(tensor_fp, dtype=INT4, block_size=32, scale_dtype=F16, symmetric=True)` accepting FP32, FP16, and BF16 inputs. - **FR-2.2** **Symmetric mode (default):**   - Per block, compute `absmax = max(|x|)` over the block.   - `scale = absmax / 7` (signed range `[-8, 7]` mapped symmetrically to `[-7, 7]`); if `absmax == 0`, `scale = 1.0` (avoid NaN/Inf).   - `q = clamp(round(x / scale), -8, 7)`. - **FR-2.3** **Asymmetric mode:**   - Per block, compute `min` and `max`; `scale = (max - min) / 15`; `zero_point = clamp(round(-min / scale), 0, 15)`; `q = clamp(round(x / scale) + zero_point, 0, 15)`.   - If `scale == 0` (constant block), `scale = 1.0`, `zero_point = 0`, and `q = 0`. - **FR-2.4** Rounding must use round-half-to-even and must be deterministic and platform-independent (no reliance on FMA-contaminated intermediates): compute `x / scale` in the scale's precision. - **FR-2.5** Quantization must support arbitrary tensor shapes, including non-multiples of the block size. The final partial block must be padded logically (zero-filled) and must not affect the scale of that block beyond the values actually present (scale computed only over real elements of the block). - **FR-2.6** Quantization must not modify the source tensor.  ### FR-3: Dequantization  - **FR-3.1** Provide `dequantize(tensor_int4, dtype=FP16|FP32|BF16)`. - **FR-3.2** Dequantization must reproduce the affine mapping used at quantization time:   - Symmetric: `x = q * scale`.   - Asymmetric: `x = (q - zero_point) * scale`. - **FR-3.3** The target output dtype must be honored exactly; no implicit promotion to FP32 unless requested. - **FR-3.4** Dequantization must be bit-exact and reproducible across runs and platforms (no re-quantization or scale re-computation).  ### FR-4: Round-trip and Accuracy Guarantees  - **FR-4.1** `dequantize(quantize(x))` must satisfy a relative error bound of `max_abs_err / max_abs_x <= 1/7` per block in symmetric mode (theoretical worst case of the 4-bit grid), measured over randomized inputs across shapes and distributions (uniform, Gaussian, heavy-tailed, constant, sparse). - **FR-4.2** Mean-squared reconstruction error (normalized) must not exceed `0.5 × (1/7)^2` of the source variance for symmetric mode on Gaussian data. - **FR-4.3** A constant-valued block must reconstruct to exactly that constant value (within `1e-3` relative) — no drift or NaN. - **FR-4.4** Round-trip through serialization (save → load → dequantize) must be bit-identical to round-trip through memory only.  ### FR-5: Storage Layout and Serialization  - **FR-5.1** Packed representation: two 4-bit values per byte; within a byte, the element with the even index occupies the **low** nibble and the element with the odd index occupies the **high** nibble. - **FR-5.2** Blocks are contiguous along the **last (innermost) dimension** of the tensor; scales/zero-points are stored in block order in a separate region. - **FR-5.3** The serialized container must store, per INT4 tensor: element count, shape, block size, scale dtype, symmetric/asymmetric flag, presence of zero-points, and the packed payload, in a self-describing header that can be parsed without the original framework. - **FR-5.4** Scale and zero-point regions must be aligned to their natural boundaries and, where the format permits, aligned to 16/32-byte boundaries for efficient loading. - **FR-5.5** Loading an INT4 tensor must validate all metadata (block size > 0, supported scale dtype, payload size consistent with element count and block count) and raise a clear, actionable error on mismatch. - **FR-5.6** Existing model files containing INT4 tensors must remain loadable by older readers that ignore unknown types, or the format must provide an explicit, documented version/compatibility policy (e.g., a format version bump plus a conversion tool).  ### FR-6: Kernel / Operator Support  - **FR-6.1** Provide a vectorized dequantization kernel for `INT4 → FP16` and `INT4 → FP32` producing results identical to FR-3.2. - **FR-6.2** Provide a fused weight-only quantized matmul (or equivalent linear op) accepting INT4 weights with INT8/FP16 activations, where the project already offers INT8 weight-only paths. If no fused kernel is available, the framework must transparently fall back to dequantize-then-matmul with identical numerical results within the accuracy bounds of FR-4. - **FR-6.3** Quantization itself must be implemented with a parallelized kernel (multi-threaded / SIMD where available) to avoid being the bottleneck during model conversion. - **FR-6.4** Any op that does not natively accept INT4 must either (a) dequantize implicitly with no silent precision surprises, or (b) raise an explicit unsupported-type error. Silent reinterpretation of INT4 bytes as INT8 is forbidden.  ### FR-7: API and Usability  - **FR-7.1** Public API surface must include: dtype constant/`enum`, `quantize`, `dequantize`, and a way to inspect INT4 tensor metadata (`block_size`, `scale_dtype`, `symmetric`, `zero_point`). - **FR-7.2** Python bindings must allow `torch.zeros(..., dtype=int4)`-style construction where the backend supports it, plus `tensor.to(torch.int4)` and `tensor.dequantize()`. - **FR-7.3** A CLI utility must support: converting an existing checkpoint/weight file to INT4, verifying/inspecting INT4 tensors in a file, and reporting per-tensor reconstruction error. - **FR-7.4** Documentation must state the exact format, defaults, error bounds, and usage examples for both symmetric and asymmetric modes. - **FR-7.5** Configuration via project config files and environment variables (e.g., block size, scale dtype) must be supported consistently with existing precision options.  ### FR-8: Error Handling and Validation  - **FR-8.1** Attempting to quantize a non-floating-point tensor must raise a clear error naming the source dtype. - **FR-8.2** Attempting to dequantize a non-INT4 tensor, or to quantize with an invalid block size (≤ 0 or non-power-of-two where power-of-two is required), must raise a descriptive error. - **FR-8.3** Loading a corrupt or truncated INT4 payload must fail with an error identifying the tensor and offset, not with undefined behavior or a segfault. - **FR-8.4** All INT4 code paths must be free of undefined behavior, out-of-bounds reads (including the final partial block and nibble extraction), and integer overflow.  ## 6. Non-Functional Requirements  - **NFR-1 (Performance):** Dequantization throughput must be at least 2 GB/s of packed INT4 payload per core on the reference CPU (AVX2-class), and at least 10 GB/s on the reference GPU. - **NFR-2 (Memory):** An INT4 tensor must occupy exactly `ceil(n / 2) + n/block_size * scale_bytes (+ n/block_size * zero_point_bytes)` bytes, excluding container overhead; no hidden FP copy retained after quantization. - **NFR-3 (Compatibility):** No regression in existing INT8/FP16/FP32 numerics, test pass rate, or file-format compatibility. - **NFR-4 (Portability):** Byte layout must be platform-independent (defined little-endian, fixed nibble order), so files produced on one platform load identically on another. - **NFR-5 (Determinism):** Identical inputs must produce byte-identical quantized payloads across runs, threads, and platforms. - **NFR-6 (Code Quality):** Implementation must pass the project's linting, formatting, static analysis, and code-coverage thresholds; new code must be covered by unit tests. - **NFR-7 (Footprint):** Library binary size increase attributable to INT4 support must not exceed 10% of the current release size.  ## 7. Acceptance Criteria  1. `INT4` appears in the dtype registry and can be selected by name in all supported configuration surfaces. 2. `quantize` / `dequantize` round-trip passes the error bounds in FR-4 across the defined test matrix (≥ 100 randomized shapes/dtypes, including non-multiple-of-block-size shapes). 3. Asymmetric mode round-trips within `1/15` relative error per block; symmetric within `1/7`. 4. A saved and reloaded INT4 tensor dequantizes to bit-identical values. 5. The fused INT4 weight-only matmul matches the dequantize-then-matmul reference within the tolerance of the reference path. 6. The conversion CLI can convert an existing checkpoint to INT4 and report per-tensor error, and the result loads in a fresh process. 7. All existing tests continue to pass; new INT4 unit and integration tests are present and green. 8. Documentation describes the format, defaults, and usage.  ## 8. Open Questions / Decisions to Confirm  - Default block size: **32** (aligns with common 4-bit GGML-style layouts) vs. 64 or 128 (better accuracy, coarser scales) — confirm against the project's target model families. - Default scale dtype: **F16** vs. F32 (accuracy vs. size). - Whether to support INT4 **activations** in the first release or restrict to weights only. - Whether to accept external GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF 4-bit checkpoints directly, or only convert from the project's native formats. - Whether the asymmetric zero-point is required for the first release or can be deferred.

requirement: ## Requirement: `reflect` — Add a `NamedOf` reflection helper  ### 1. Summary  The reflection layer currently exposes raw `ReflectionType` instances (`ReflectionNamedType`, `ReflectionUnionType`, `ReflectionIntersectionType`) to consumers, forcing every call site to re-implement the same non-trivial logic:  * determining whether a type is a *named* type (as opposed to a union or intersection), * extracting the underlying `ReflectionNamedType` from a nullable/union/intersection wrapper, * resolving the pseudo-types `self`, `parent`, and `static` into a real class name.  This logic is duplicated across parameter, return-type and property-type handling, and is easy to get wrong (e.g. treating `?string` as a union, or returning the literal `"self"` instead of the declaring class).  Add a first-class, dependency-free helper named **`NamedOf`** to the `reflect` component that encapsulates this behaviour and is used internally wherever named-type extraction is required.  ### 2. Location / Namespace  ``` Reflect\NamedOf ```  (placed in the existing `reflect` component alongside the other reflection utilities; the concrete namespace prefix of the component is to follow the project's existing conventions).  ### 3. Public API  ```php final class NamedOf {     /**      * Returns the underlying ReflectionNamedType of $type, or null if $type      * is not a named type (or does not contain exactly one named type).      */     public static function of(?ReflectionType $type): ?ReflectionNamedType;      /**      * Returns the fully-qualified name of the named type of $type, or null      * if $type is not a named type.      */     public static function name(?ReflectionType $type): ?string;      /**      * Returns true if $type is (or contains exactly) a named type.      */     public static function isNamed(?ReflectionType $type): bool; } ```  The class must be `final`, stateless, and contain no instance state. All methods must be callable statically; no constructor arguments, no configuration, and no service-container registration are required.  ### 4. Behaviour Specification  #### 4.1 `of()`  | Input | Output | |---|---| | `ReflectionNamedType` for `int`, `string`, `array`, `callable`, `iterable`, `object`, `mixed`, `void`, `never`, `false`, `true`, `null` | the same instance | | `ReflectionNamedType` for `self` / `parent` / `static` | the same instance (name resolution is performed by `name()`) | | Nullable named type (`?Foo` — i.e. `allowsNull() === true` on a `ReflectionNamedType`) | the same instance | | `ReflectionUnionType` containing exactly one named type (e.g. `Foo|null` as emitted by some reflection implementations) | that named type | | `ReflectionUnionType` containing more than one named type (e.g. `Foo|Bar`) | `null` | | `ReflectionIntersectionType` containing exactly one named type | that named type | | `ReflectionIntersectionType` containing more than one named type | `null` | | `null` (no type declared) | `null` |  `of()` must never throw for any valid `ReflectionType` input.  #### 4.2 `name()`  * Returns `getName()` verbatim for builtin types (`int`, `string`, `bool`, `float`, `array`, `callable`, `iterable`, `object`, `mixed`, `void`, `never`, `false`, `true`, `null`). * For `self` and `static`, returns the fully-qualified name of the class in whose scope the type was declared. * For `parent`, returns the fully-qualified name of the parent of the declaring class, or `null` if the declaring class has no parent. * Class names are returned fully qualified (leading `\` stripped, i.e. `App\Domain\User`, not `\App\Domain\User`). * Returns `null` in every case in which `of()` returns `null`, and for a `null` input.  #### 4.3 `isNamed()`  * Returns `true` exactly when `of()` returns a non-`null` value.  ### 5. Integration  * The existing internal code paths that currently inspect `ReflectionNamedType` / `ReflectionUnionType` / `ReflectionIntersectionType` manually must be refactored to delegate to `NamedOf`, removing duplicated branching. * The helper must not alter the behaviour of existing public APIs; this is an additive change.  ### 6. Non-functional Requirements  * **No new runtime dependencies.** The implementation may only use PHP's native `Reflection*` classes. * **PHP version compatibility:** must run on the minimum PHP version supported by the project (no use of features newer than that, e.g. `ReflectionUnionType`/`ReflectionIntersectionType` must be feature-detected before use). * **Performance:** `of()` / `name()` must not perform repeated reflection instantiation for the same input within a single call; where a class name must be resolved for `self`/`parent`/`static`, an existing cached reflection instance should be reused rather than re-created per call. * **Type safety:** all parameters and return values must be strictly typed and declared.  ### 7. Acceptance Criteria  1. `NamedOf::of()` / `NamedOf::name()` / `NamedOf::isNamed()` exist with the signatures in §3 and are publicly accessible. 2. Unit tests cover every row of the tables in §4, including `?Foo`, `Foo|null`, `Foo|Bar`, `A&B`, `self`, `parent`, `static`, builtin types, and `null` input. 3. A test asserts that `self`/`static` resolve to the declaring class name and that `parent` resolves to the parent class name. 4. A test asserts that `name()` returns `null` for `Foo|Bar` and for a `null` input. 5. Existing test suite continues to pass with no regressions; duplicated named-type branching is removed from the component. 6. Public API documentation / changelog entry added describing `NamedOf` and its resolution rules.

requirement: ## Requirement: Multiple Window Support for Desktop Shells  ### Problem The desktop shell currently supports only a single window/instance of its hosted content. Applications built on the shell cannot present more than one view, cannot open a second window (e.g., a preferences dialog, a detached document, or a split view), and cannot programmatically close, focus, or query existing windows. This limits the shell to simple single-view applications.  ### Scope The desktop shell component (the native window layer used to host the application's web/UI content) must support managing multiple windows concurrently, each fully independent.  ### Functional Requirements 1. **Window creation** — The shell must expose an API to create a new window with a configurable set of options (initial URL/route, size, position, title, resizability, parent/child relationship, and whether it is shown on creation). Each call must return a handle (window identifier) that can be used for subsequent operations. 2. **Multiple concurrent instances** — Two or more windows must be able to exist at the same time. Each window must have its own isolated content context (separate session/storage where the underlying engine allows it) and its own navigation, title, and lifecycle state. Content in one window must not affect or replace the content of another. 3. **Window enumeration** — The shell must allow querying the list of currently open windows and retrieving metadata (identifier, title, URL, bounds, focus state) for each. 4. **Window lifecycle control** — The shell must allow programmatically closing a specific window, focusing/raising a specific window, showing/hiding a window, and resizing/repositioning it. 5. **Focus and activation** — Exactly one window may be focused at a time. Creating, closing, or focusing a window must update the OS-level focus/active-window state accordingly, and focus events must be reported to the application. 6. **Cleanup on close** — Closing a window must release its associated resources (process/web-view instances, event listeners, IPC channels) and remove it from the window list. No orphaned resources or dangling event handlers may remain. 7. **Events / notifications** — The shell must emit events for window creation, close, focus change, resize, and navigation, including the affected window identifier. 8. **Backward compatibility** — Existing applications that rely on the current single-window behavior (including any "main window" accessors) must continue to work unchanged. The first/primary window may remain addressable via a convenience accessor or option (e.g., `isMain`), and applications that never create an additional window must observe identical behavior to before. 9. **Configuration** — The shell's configuration must permit specifying the initial window(s) to create at startup, including the ability to start with more than one window.  ### Non-functional Requirements - Window operations must not block the UI/event loop; window creation and closure must be safe to call from multiple threads/tasks. - Performance and memory footprint must not degrade when only a single window is used (the common case). - The implementation must work on all desktop platforms supported by the shell (Windows, macOS, Linux) with consistent semantics.  ### Acceptance Criteria - An application can create a second window at runtime; both windows render their own content simultaneously and remain independently navigable. - Creating a window does not close, replace, or blank the existing window. - Closing one window leaves the others open and fully functional, and the shell's window list is updated. - Focusing a specific window brings it to the foreground and marks it as the active window; focus events fire for both the newly focused and previously focused window. - Enumerating windows returns exactly the set of currently open windows with correct metadata. - After closing a window, no events are delivered for it and its resources are released. - Existing single-window applications continue to build and run without modification, with no behavioral change. - Automated tests exist covering: creating multiple windows, isolation of content/state, focus switching, closing, enumeration, and backward-compatible single-window behavior.
explanation: The requirement is detailed and mostly clear with precise API descriptions and testable acceptance criteria, making it highly unambiguous and verifiable; however it bundles many distinct capabilities (creation, enumeration, lifecycle, focus, events, backward compatibility, configuration) into a single requirement, reducing its singularity.

requirement: ## Requirement: Optimize the `format_args!` macro  ### Problem  The `format_args!` macro, which builds a `std::fmt::Arguments` value for use with formatting APIs such as `format!`, `write!`, `println!`, and `panic!`, is currently expensive. Expanding it produces a large amount of generated code (format-spec parsing machinery, per-argument handler thunks, and a stack-allocated `Arguments`/`Pieces` structure), which increases compile times, bloats binary size, and imposes measurable runtime overhead even for trivial format strings such as `format_args!("hello")` or `format_args!("{}", x)`.  ### Requirement  `format_args!` must be reworked so that constructing a `fmt::Arguments` value is effectively free unless formatting actually takes place, while preserving all observable behavior.  Specifically:  1. **Low-overhead expansion** — the code generated for a `format_args!` invocation must be substantially smaller than today. The common cases (no arguments, a single literal string, and a small number of primitive arguments) must not emit the full generic formatting machinery. 2. **No unnecessary work at construction time** — building the `Arguments` value must not perform format-string parsing, allocation, or handler dispatch eagerly. Parsing of the format string must be done at compile time wherever possible, and any remaining runtime work must be proportional to the actual formatting performed. 3. **Cheap common paths** — formatting a `Arguments` value that contains only literal text, or text plus simple primitive types, should avoid dynamic dispatch and heap allocation, and should be measurably faster than the current implementation. 4. **Preserved semantics** — the following must remain unchanged:    - All existing formatting traits and specifiers behave identically, including `{}`, `{0}`, named arguments, width/precision, `{:?}`, `{:#?}`, `{:x}`, `{:#x}`, fill/align, and custom `Display`/`Debug`/`LowerHex`/`UpperHex` implementations.    - The lifetime and borrow semantics of the produced `fmt::Arguments` (borrowing from the format string and the arguments) are unchanged.    - Compile-time errors for malformed format strings are still reported, and error messages remain helpful.    - `format_args!` results may still be stored in a `let` binding and passed to functions taking `fmt::Arguments`, and may still be used directly as a formatting argument. 5. **Compatibility** — the optimization must not require changes to user code and must not break downstream crates, `no_std` targets, or `const`-context usage patterns that are currently supported.  ### Success criteria  - Benchmarks of `format!`/`write!`/`println!`-style calls with 0–3 arguments show a clear reduction in runtime and in allocation count compared to the current implementation. - Binary size of a program using `format_args!` in typical ways is reduced. - Compile time of crates using `format!`/`println!` extensively is reduced. - The existing test suite, including formatting-trait and compile-fail tests, passes unchanged.
explanation: The requirement is detailed and mostly clear, with precise goals and success criteria, though some terms like "substantially smaller" and "measurably faster" are vague, leaving minor ambiguity. It provides concrete verification methods (benchmarks, binary size, tests), making it verifiable, but lacks exact numeric thresholds. It bundles multiple distinct optimization goals (code size, parsing, performance, semantics, compatibility), so it is not singular.

requirement: # Requirement: Set Collection Primitive  **ID:** REQ-SET-001 **Title:** Implement a `Set` primitive as a first-class collection type, complementary to the existing `Dictionary` and `Array` primitives **Status:** Draft for implementation  ---  ## 1. Motivation  The runtime currently provides `Array` (ordered, indexable sequence) and `Dictionary` (unordered key→value mapping) as its only built-in collection types. There is no dedicated primitive for representing an unordered collection of unique elements. Users are forced to emulate sets with `Array` + linear `contains` scans (O(n) membership) or with `Dictionary` using dummy values (exposing meaningless keys/values through the public API).  A first-class `Set` primitive removes these workarounds, enables O(1) average membership testing, provides standard set algebra, and makes intent explicit in user code and in the type signatures of standard-library functions.  ---  ## 2. Scope  ### 2.1 In scope - A new built-in `Set` value type, implemented in the runtime core (not as a user-space library), with parity in native support, GC integration, and interop with `Array`/`Dictionary`. - Creation, mutation, and inspection operations. - Set algebra (union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference) and relation predicates. - Element hashing/equality rules consistent with those used by `Dictionary` keys. - Functional operations (`map`, `filter`, `reduce`) that return the appropriate collection type. - Conversion to and from `Array` and `Dictionary`. - Literal and constructor syntax. - Serialization/deserialization support in the standard JSON/text codecs. - Interop rules with `Array` and `Dictionary` (membership testing, equality comparison, spread/iteration). - Documentation and language reference updates.  ### 2.2 Out of scope - Ordered/sorted sets, multi-sets (bags), and set-with-expiry. - Mutable keys, thread-safety guarantees beyond the runtime's existing synchronization model for `Dictionary`/`Array`. - New hash algorithms; `Set` must reuse the runtime's existing hash/equality implementation.  ---  ## 3. Functional Requirements  ### 3.1 Construction | Requirement | Detail | |---|---| | FR-1.1 | `Set()` creates an empty set. | | FR-1.2 | `Set(iterable)` creates a set from any iterable whose elements are hashable; duplicate elements are collapsed, keeping the first occurrence. | | FR-1.3 | `Set(arrayLike)` must accept `Array` and any other iterable, and must accept another `Set` (producing an independent copy). | | FR-1.4 | A literal form (e.g. `#{a, b, c}`, syntax to match host-language conventions) desugars to `Set` construction with constant-folded contents. An empty literal yields an empty set. | | FR-1.5 | `Set` values are value-like with copy-on-write semantics: assigning a set to a variable or inserting it into a container must not allow aliasing to mutate both. |  ### 3.2 Core operations | ID | Operation | Contract | |---|---|---| | FR-2.1 | `add(element)` | Inserts `element` if absent. Returns `true` if the element was added, `false` if it was already present. No-op on duplicates. | | FR-2.2 | `remove(element)` | Removes `element` if present; returns `true` if removed, `false` otherwise. | | FR-2.3 | `discard(element)` | Removes `element` if present, otherwise does nothing; never raises for missing elements. | | FR-2.4 | `contains(element)` | Returns `true` if `element` is a member. Average O(1). | | FR-2.5 | `size` / `count` | Number of distinct elements; O(1). | | FR-2.6 | `isEmpty` | `true` when the set has no elements. | | FR-2.7 | `clear()` | Removes all elements; sets `size` to 0. | | FR-2.8 | `copy()` | Returns an independent shallow copy of the set. | | FR-2.9 | `toArray()` | Returns an `Array` of the elements. Order must be documented (see §4.3). | | FR-2.10 | `toDictionary()` | Returns a `Dictionary` mapping each element to `true` (or the documented sentinel), enabling idiomatic value lookups. | | FR-2.11 | `union(other)` / `intersection(other)` / `difference(other)` / `symmetricDifference(other)` | Return a **new** `Set`; operands are not mutated. `other` may be a `Set` or any iterable. | | FR-2.12 | `isSubsetOf(other)` / `isSupersetOf(other)` / `isDisjointWith(other)` / `isEqualTo(other)` | Return booleans. | | FR-2.13 | `map(fn)` | Returns an `Array` of `fn` applied to each element. | | FR-2.14 | `filter(predicate)` | Returns a new `Set` of elements satisfying `predicate`. | | FR-2.15 | `reduce(initial, fn)` | Left fold over elements in iteration order; returns the accumulator. | | FR-2.16 | `forEach(fn)` | Invokes `fn(element)` once per element in iteration order. | | FR-2.17 | `pop()`/`removeFirst()` (if the host `Array` exposes such mutators) | Removes and returns an arbitrary element, or `nil`/`null` when empty — semantics and naming must match the existing `Array`/`Dictionary` mutator conventions. |  ### 3.3 Interop and language integration - **FR-3.1** `element in someSet` and `someSet contains element` are both supported and equivalent. - **FR-3.2** `Set` is iterable (usable in `for` loops and spread into `Set(...)`, `Array(...)`). - **FR-3.3** Set algebra is also expressible via operator syntax where the language supports operator overloading (e.g. `|`, `&`, `-`, `^`), and these operators must have the same semantics as the named methods. - **FR-3.4** Equality: two sets are equal iff they contain the same elements, regardless of insertion order. - **FR-3.5** `Set` participates in `==`/`!=` comparison with `Array`/`Dictionary` by returning `false` (no cross-type coercion), except that `Set` vs. `Set` uses set equality. - **FR-3.6** A `Set` may be used as a `Dictionary` key only if the set is immutable/frozen per the runtime's existing rules for hashable keys; the runtime must produce a documented, deterministic error otherwise. - **FR-3.7** Standard-library functions that accept "any iterable collection" (e.g. `join`, `flatten`, `unique`, `groupBy`) must accept `Set` without modification. - **FR-3.8** A `unique()` (or equivalent) helper on `Array` should be implementable by delegating to `Set` internally.  ### 3.4 Error handling | ID | Condition | Required behavior | |---|---|---| | FR-4.1 | Element is unhashable (e.g. an `Array`, `Dictionary`, function, or other non-hashable value) | Raise the runtime's standard type error (`TypeError`), naming `Set` and the offending type. Must not crash the process or corrupt the set. | | FR-4.2 | Operation receives a non-iterable argument where an iterable is required | Raise the standard type error. | | FR-4.3 | `remove` on an absent element | Must not raise; return `false` (per FR-2.2). If the host convention requires `remove` to raise on missing keys (as `Dictionary.remove` may), `Set.remove` must match that convention and the behavior must be documented and tested. | | FR-4.4 | Errors raised during iteration (e.g. element mutated during `forEach`) | Must follow the runtime's existing invalidation semantics for `Dictionary`/`Array`. |  ---  ## 4. Non-Functional Requirements  ### 4.1 Performance - **NFR-1.1** `contains`, `add`, `remove` must be O(1) average time, using the same hashing strategy and open-addressing/chaining design as `Dictionary`. - **NFR-1.2** `add` of an existing element must be O(1) and must not grow the backing storage. - **NFR-1.3** Set algebra operations must be O(n + m) in the sizes of the operands. - **NFR-1.4** `Set` must not be more than 2× the memory footprint of an equivalent `Dictionary` with the same elements.  ### 4.2 Correctness and consistency - **NFR-2.1** Hash/equality semantics for elements must be identical to `Dictionary` key semantics: `a == b` ⇒ `hash(a) == hash(b)`, and elements that compare equal are treated as the same member. - **NFR-2.2** The implementation must pass the runtime's existing conformance suite for collections plus a new dedicated `Set` test suite. - **NFR-2.3** No regressions in `Array`/`Dictionary` performance or behavior (benchmark suite must show no statistically significant regression).  ### 4.3 Determinism - **NFR-3.1** Iteration order must be deterministic and documented: either insertion order is preserved, or a stable but unspecified order derived from the hash table is used. The chosen order must be stable across runs for the same insertion sequence and must not change when an unrelated element is added or removed (if hash-order is chosen, removal-induced rehash effects must not reorder unaffected elements — e.g. use tombstones rather than re-inserting).  ### 4.4 Serialization - **NFR-4.1** JSON/text encoders must encode `Set` as a JSON array of its elements in iteration order. - **NFR-4.2** Decoders must accept a JSON array and produce a `Set`, collapsing duplicates. - **NFR-4.3** Round-trip encode→decode must yield an equal set.  ### 4.5 Portability and API stability - **NFR-5.1** `Set` must be implemented in the runtime core with the same cross-platform support matrix as `Array`/`Dictionary` (all supported architectures/interpreters). - **NFR-5.2** The public API must be documented in the language reference, and the feature must be covered by a versioned API-stability note.  ---  ## 5. Acceptance Criteria  1. `Set` is a built-in type constructible via `Set()`, `Set(iterable)`, and literal syntax, with no imports required. 2. All operations in §3.2 are implemented, behave as specified, and are covered by unit tests — including edge cases: empty set, single element, duplicate insertion, removal of absent element, self-union/intersection/difference, `difference` with a superset, symmetric difference, sets of mixed element types, and sets containing `nil`/`null` (if `nil` is hashable in the host language). 3. `contains` returns `true`/`false` exactly for members; membership is consistent with `Dictionary` key lookup for the same element. 4. Attempting to add an unhashable element raises a `TypeError` with a clear message and leaves the set unmodified. 5. Set equality is order-independent; `Set([1,2]) == Set([2,1])` is `true`. 6. `Array`/`Dictionary`/spread/`for` iteration over a `Set` works, and existing standard-library collection functions accept `Set` arguments. 7. JSON round-trip of a `Set` preserves its contents. 8. Benchmarks show `contains` on a 100k-element set is at least 100× faster than the equivalent linear `Array` scan. 9. The full existing test suite passes with no regressions; new `Set` tests achieve full coverage of the added code paths. 10. Documentation (language reference + standard-library API docs) is updated, including element hashability rules, iteration-order guarantees, and error behavior.  ---  ## 6. Deliverables  - Core `Set` type implementation (runtime + GC/ownership integration). - Built-in constructor, literal syntax, and parser/desugaring support. - Interop with `Array`, `Dictionary`, iterators, and operator syntax. - JSON/text (de)serialization support. - Unit, conformance, and property-based tests (e.g. algebraic laws: `A ∪ B = B ∪ A`, `A ∩ B ⊆ A`, `A \ A = ∅`, `A △ A = ∅`, De Morgan identities). - Benchmarks comparing `Set` vs. `Array`-based emulation. - Language reference and API documentation updates.
explanation: The requirement is extensively detailed with explicit contracts, making it largely unambiguous; only a few points (e.g., iteration order, literal syntax) leave room for interpretation. It provides measurable criteria (O(1) operations, benchmarks, test cases) and clear acceptance criteria, so it is highly verifiable. However, it encompasses many distinct capabilities (construction, core operations, algebra, interop, serialization, etc.), which means it is not a single, focused requirement, resulting in a low singularity score.

requirement: ## Requirement: Union Types in Typed GDScript  ### Summary Extend Typed GDScript's static type system to support **union types** — annotations that declare a value may hold any one of several types — while preserving existing behavior for non-union code and keeping runtime performance unchanged.  ### 1. Syntax - A union type is written by joining two or more type names with the `|` operator in any type-annotation position:   ```gdscript   var health: int | float = 100   var state: String | int = "idle"   var mixed: int | float | String | Color   ``` - Union types must be accepted in:   - Local variable and constant declarations   - Class member variable declarations (exported and non-exported)   - Function parameter types   - Function return types - `Variant` may appear as a union member and acts as a catch-all (`int | Variant` is equivalent to `Variant`). - Union members may be built-in types, script classes, or other valid GDScript type names; nested unions and unions containing arrays are not required in the initial implementation and should produce a clear parse error rather than a crash.  ### 2. Compile-time type checking - Assigning a value to a union-typed target is valid only if the value's type is compatible with **at least one** union member; otherwise a compile-time error is raised with a message listing the union members and the given type. - When a value is compatible with multiple members, the most specific matching member is used for inference purposes (e.g. `int` is chosen over `float` for an integer literal in an `int | float` union). - Numeric widening rules apply within unions: an `int` value is assignable to `int | float` but a `float` value is **not** assignable to `int | float`. - Default values in declarations with union types must be compatible with at least one member. - Function calls must reject arguments whose types match no union member of the corresponding parameter, and return values that match no member of a union return type must raise a runtime type error consistent with existing typed-GDScript behavior.  ### 3. Inference and preservation of existing typing - Code without union annotations must behave exactly as before: `var x = 5` still infers `int`, not `Variant`. - Declaring a union type must not silently degrade the variable to untyped `Variant`; the declared union is retained for static checking, tooltips, and documentation.  ### 4. Type narrowing - Within an `if`/`elif` block guarded by `is` checks against union members, the variable must be narrowed to the matching member so that member-specific operations (method calls, property access) are allowed without unsafe-access warnings:   ```gdscript   var value: int | String = "hi"   if value is String:       print(value.length())  # valid: narrowed to String   ``` - Narrowing must apply to the guarded block and to the negative branch (`else`, or `if not value is String`), and must be invalidated when the variable is reassigned.  ### 5. Unsafe access - Accessing a method or property that exists on only some union members outside of a narrowing context must produce a warning (or error, matching the project's existing strictness settings) rather than silently failing at runtime.  ### 6. Casting - The `as` operator must support union types, allowing a cast to a union member and a cast to the union type itself.  ### 7. Editor and tooling support - Hovering/tooltips and generated documentation must display union types in a readable form (e.g. `int | String`). - Autocomplete and "Change Type" dialogs must handle union annotations without errors or data loss.  ### 8. Runtime behavior - Union types introduce no per-frame or per-operation overhead beyond the type checks already performed by typed GDScript; union values are stored as regular `Variant` values at runtime. - Memory usage and serialization formats are unaffected.  ### 9. Acceptance criteria - All examples above compile and run correctly in the engine and in the editor. - Invalid assignments, invalid call arguments, and invalid narrowing produce clear, actionable error messages. - The full existing GDScript test suite continues to pass with no regressions, and new tests cover parsing, assignment checking, narrowing, casting, and error reporting for union types.
explanation: The requirement is detailed and largely unambiguous with clear syntax and rules, though some notions like “most specific matching member” could be interpreted differently. However, it bundles many distinct capabilities (syntax, inference, narrowing, casting, tooling, runtime) rather than focusing on a single feature, lowering its singularity score.

requirement: **Requirement: Array Unpacking (Destructuring) in GDScript**  **Summary:** GDScript shall support destructuring assignment that unpacks the elements of an `Array` into multiple variables in a single statement.  **Functional Requirements**  1. **Variable declaration unpacking:** The language shall allow `var [a, b, c] = expression`, where each identifier in the bracketed pattern is bound to the element at the corresponding zero-based index of the right-hand `Array`. 2. **Assignment unpacking:** The language shall allow `[a, b] = expression` to assign to existing variables, members, or subscripted targets (e.g., `self.x`, `arr[0]`) without declaring new variables. 3. **Swap idiom:** `[a, b] = [b, a]` shall swap the values of `a` and `b` correctly, with the right-hand side fully evaluated before any assignment occurs. 4. **Ignored elements:** The wildcard identifier `_` in a pattern shall skip the corresponding element without binding it to a variable. Multiple `_` entries shall be permitted. 5. **Rest element:** A single rest element, written `..rest` or an equivalent agreed syntax, shall bind the remaining elements to a new `Array`. It shall be permitted only once and only in the final position. 6. **Nested patterns:** Patterns shall support nesting for arrays of arrays, e.g., `var [x, [y, z]] = data`. 7. **Iteration support:** Patterns shall be usable as the loop variable in `for [k, v] in array_of_pairs:` so that each iterated element is unpacked. 8. **Return-value compatibility:** Destructuring shall work with any expression yielding an `Array`, including function calls and `yield`/`await` results.  **Error Handling Requirements**  9. **Non-array source:** If the right-hand value is not an `Array` at runtime, the engine shall raise a runtime error that includes the script path, line number, and the actual type received, and shall not partially assign any target. 10. **Length mismatch:** If the source array has fewer elements than the pattern requires (excluding a rest element), the engine shall raise a runtime error and perform no assignments. If the source has more elements than the pattern and no rest element is present, the extra elements shall be silently ignored, consistent with a documented behavior. 11. **Compile-time checks:** The parser shall report a syntax error for malformed patterns, including duplicate rest elements, a rest element not in the final position, and empty patterns. 12. **Duplicate names:** Declaring the same identifier twice in one declaration pattern shall produce a compile-time error, except for `_`.  **Compatibility Requirements**  13. **No breaking changes:** Existing valid GDScript that begins a statement with `[` (array literal expressions, subscript chains on literals) shall continue to parse and execute with identical semantics. Destructuring shall not create intermediate `Array` copies beyond what is required for the rest element. Unpacking a fixed-size pattern shall perform element reads directly from the source array.  **Documentation Requirements**  17. The GDScript reference shall document the syntax, the rest and wildcard semantics, the error conditions listed above, and at least one example for each of declaration, assignment, swap, and loop usage.  **Acceptance Criteria**  - All functional requirements have unit tests in the GDScript test suite. - Error conditions 9 through 12 produce the specified diagnostics with correct line numbers. - The existing GDScript test suite passes unchanged (requirement 13). - The swap idiom and nested patterns are verified with tests covering object properties and subscripted targets.

requirement: **Requirement: DistributedDataParallel (DDP) Support in the PyTorch C++ API (libtorch)**  **Overview** The PyTorch C++ API (libtorch) shall provide a DistributedDataParallel (DDP) module, functionally equivalent to the Python API's `torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel`, enabling users to train neural networks with distributed data parallelism entirely in C++.  **Background** Distributed data-parallel training is currently accessible only from Python. C++ users must embed the Python interpreter, hand-roll gradient synchronization, or forgo distributed training. Libtorch already ships the low-level `c10d` process group primitives (Gloo, MPI, NCCL backends) but lacks the higher-level DDP synchronization layer built on top of them.  **Functional Requirements**  - **FR1 — DDP Wrapper API:** The C++ API shall expose a `DistributedDataParallel` wrapper (e.g., under `torch::nn::parallel`) that is constructible from any user-supplied `torch::nn::Module`, a `c10d::ProcessGroup` handle, and configuration options (source rank, bucket capacity, target device). - **FR2 — Replica Consistency:** At construction, the wrapper shall broadcast all model parameters and buffers from the source rank (default: rank 0) to every other rank so all replicas begin training from an identical state. - **FR3 — Automatic Gradient Synchronization:** During the backward pass, the wrapper shall automatically all-reduce gradients across all ranks in the process group, applying the reduction (e.g., averaging) before the optimizer step. - **FR4 — Overlapped Communication:** The wrapper shall bucket gradients and overlap all-reduce communication with backward computation wherever the device backend supports it. - **FR5 — Supported Scenarios:** The wrapper shall support multi-process/multi-node training, single-process multi-device training, and single-process multi-thread training, using the applicable `c10d` backends (Gloo, NCCL, MPI). - **FR6 — Gradient Accumulation:** The wrapper shall provide a mechanism to disable gradient synchronization for a given iteration (equivalent of Python's `no_sync()`) to support gradient accumulation. - **FR7 — Drop-in Usage:** The wrapper shall forward calls to the wrapped module and expose its parameters and sub-modules (including optimizer access), acting as a drop-in replacement for the base module in C++ training loops. - **FR8 — Error Diagnostics:** Collective communication failures and misuse (e.g., inconsistent model definitions across ranks, uninitialized process group) shall produce clear, informative error messages.  **Non-Functional Requirements**  - **NFR1 — API Parity:** Naming, defaults, and semantics shall match the Python DDP implementation to allow straightforward migration. - **NFR2 — Performance:** End-to-end training throughput with the C++ wrapper shall not regress by more than 10% relative to the Python DDP on a standard benchmark model. - **NFR3 — Documentation and Testing:** The feature shall include C++ API documentation, at least one end-to-end example in the C++ examples directory, and unit/integration tests covering multi-process and multi-GPU configurations.  **Acceptance Criteria**  1. A C++ training program using the wrapper trains a model across N processes/nodes and achieves convergence and metrics equivalent to the Python DDP training on identical data and hyperparameters. 2. Model parameters remain identical across all ranks after every optimizer step. 3. Gradient accumulation with synchronization disabled yields results identical to standard synchronous training. 4. The documented example builds and runs on Linux with at least the Gloo (CPU) and NCCL (CUDA) backends.  **Dependencies / Constraints** - Builds upon the existing `c10d` C++ process group APIs in libtorch; no new communication backends are required. - Target platforms: Linux and macOS (CPU backends); Linux only for the NCCL (CUDA) backend.

requirement: **REQ-001: Transformer Input Embedding and Positional Encoding Module**  The system shall implement an input processing module that transforms discrete token sequences into continuous vector representations by combining a learnable token embedding layer with positional encodings to preserve both semantic meaning and sequence order.  **Functional Requirements:** 1. The module shall support configurable positional encoding of shape `[max_sequence_length, d_model]` using either:    - Fixed sinusoidal functions: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)) and PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)), or    - Learnable parameter vectors initialized via standard initialization schemes. 4.
